surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: Central vertigo occurs due to disruption of the balance system at the receptor level, impaired transmission by afferent pathways, or dysfunction of integration and coordination centers in the brainstem and cerebellum extending to cortical perception. Subjective symptoms include headache, lightheadedness, floating sensation, diplopia, and dysphagia. Objective findings include cold sweats, vomiting, pallor, staggering gait, and nystagmus.

surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: Central vertigo is not a standalone disease but a symptom of underlying central vestibular system pathology. Etiologies classified by onset: (1) Acute onset: vascular causes (stroke, TIA) and post-traumatic diffuse axonal injury. (2) Subacute, chronic, or episodic onset: inflammatory/infectious causes (multiple sclerosis), tumors (acoustic neuroma, medulloblastoma), epilepsy, and migraine-associated dizziness. Multiple sclerosis presents with spinning dizziness, decreased visual acuity with eye movement pain, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, blurred vision, diplopia, balance disturbance, and cranial nerve VIII involvement. Management includes corticosteroids and interferon for relapsing cases. CPA tumors present with unilateral hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, facial numbness, facial pain, headache, decreased vision, ataxia, and hemiparesis. CPA tumors most commonly involve vestibular schwannoma. Primary treatment is surgery with three categories: observation/conservative, radiotherapy/stereotactic radiosurgery, and microsurgery.

expanded_sections.heading: Anatomi Sistem Vestibularis

content_blocks.text: The vestibular system has peripheral and central components. Peripheral structures include the vestibular apparatus and vestibular nerve (cranial nerve VIII). Central structures include the brainstem (vestibular nuclei), thalamus, cerebral cortex, and cerebellum. Central vertigo specifically localizes to lesions along the central vestibular pathway from the nucleus vestibularis in the brainstem through the thalamus to the cerebral cortex.

expanded_sections.heading: Etiologi dan Manifestasi Klinis Vertigo Sentral

content_blocks.text: Central vertigo is not an independent disease but a symptom of underlying pathology affecting the central vestibular system. The etiology determines the clinical presentation and guides management.

ACUTE ONSET ETIOLOGIES: Vascular causes (stroke, TIA) and post-traumatic diffuse axonal injury are the most common acute presentations, requiring immediate neuroimaging and stroke protocol evaluation.

SUBACUTE/CHRONIC/EPISODIC ETIOLOGIES: Multiple sclerosis presents with spinning dizziness, decreased visual acuity with painful eye movements, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, blurred vision, diplopia, balance disturbance, and CN VIII involvement. Treatment involves corticosteroids and interferon for relapsing-remitting disease. CPA tumors (most commonly vestibular schwannoma) present with unilateral hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, trigeminal nerve dysfunction (facial numbness, pain), headache, vision decline, ataxia, and hemiparesis. Primary treatment is surgical, with options including observation, radiotherapy/stereotactic radiosurgery, and microsurgery. Prognosis depends on tumor size and severity of neurological deficits at diagnosis. Epilepsy vestibular type arises from focal lesions in the superior temporal gyrus or parietal association cortex receiving ipsilateral thalamic vestibular projections. Symptoms include episodic floating/rotating sensations, either as seizure aura or psychomotor seizure manifestation. Management focuses on seizure control with antiepileptic drugs. Traumatic central vertigo is a common sequela of head and neck trauma including diffuse axonal injury, presenting as central vestibular syndrome from brainstem dysfunction. Management includes pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches, with surgical intervention when indicated.

expanded_sections.subheading: Diagnostic Approach to Central Vertigo Etiology

content_blocks.text: The diagnostic workup for central vertigo should systematically evaluate for the underlying cause. Key questions include: Is central vertigo clinically confirmed? Has supportive diagnostic testing been performed? Are there differential diagnoses to consider? Once the diagnosis is established, treatment targets the specific etiology: acute stroke management, head trauma protocols, intracranial pressure reduction for infection or tumor, and other cause-specific interventions.

content_blocks.text: Symptomatic treatment aims to reduce the two main symptom clusters: the vertigo sensation (spinning, floating) and autonomic symptoms (nausea, vomiting). Vestibular suppressants are divided into three pharmacological groups.

content_blocks.text: Central vestibular vertigo requires definitive diagnosis of the underlying etiology and appropriate definitive treatment. Referral is indicated when: (1) Facilities for diagnostic confirmation and etiology-specific management are needed (e.g., suspected stroke requiring non-contrast CT head and neurology specialist consultation); (2) No improvement is seen after pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment.

expanded_sections.heading: Rehabilitasi

content_blocks.text: Rehabilitation is performed after the underlying disease has been managed and no longer poses acute health concerns requiring immediate therapy. The goals of rehabilitation are: to improve gaze stability, enhance postural body stability, prevent recurrent vertigo, and improve the patient's ability to perform daily activities independently. Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT) is a highly effective modality for improving functional deficits and subjective complaints resulting from unilateral or bilateral vestibular hypofunction and central balance disorders in both adults and children.

surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: The HIV status of a patient significantly changes the differential diagnosis for suspected brain infection. In HIV-positive patients with focal deficits, consider cerebral toxoplasmosis and tuberculoma. In HIV-negative patients with focal deficits, consider bacterial abscess and tuberculoma. expanded_sections.heading: Toksoplasma Ensefalitis

content_blocks.text: Toxoplasma encephalitis is the most common opportunistic CNS infection in immunocompromised patients in Indonesia. It results from reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii infection. Diagnosis is predominantly presumptive based on clinical probability and response to empirical therapy. Definitive diagnosis requires tissue biopsy and pathology. PCR for Toxoplasma in CSF has low sensitivity (~50%) and is not recommended as routine.

expanded_sections.heading: Meningitis Tuberkulosis

content_blocks.text: TB meningitis is difficult to diagnose because clinical symptoms are non-specific, BTA count in CSF is very low, and molecular diagnostics are not yet standard. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion in any patient with subacute fever, headache, and neurological symptoms.

The Thwaites score (Lancet 2002) helps differentiate bacterial from TB meningitis: Age >36 years (score 2), CSF WBC <900 cells/mm3 (score 3), peripheral WBC <15,000 (score 4), CSF neutrophils <75% (score 4), symptom duration >6 days (score -5). Total score >4 suggests bacterial meningitis; score <4 suggests TB meningitis.
MRC Grading: Grade I - fully conscious, no focal deficits; Grade IIa - GCS 15 with focal deficit; Grade IIb - GCS 10-14 with/without focal deficit; Grade III - GCS <10 with/without focal deficit.

Treatment: OAT for 9-12 months. First two weeks are 'life-saving.' Dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks is beneficial for HIV-negative patients (per meta-analysis). Vitamin B6 3x10mg po protects against OAT neurotoxicity. All patients with hydrocephalus or brain-spinal tuberculoma should be considered for surgical intervention.

content_blocks.text: Cryptococcal meningitis is generally opportunistic. Clinical presentation is subacute over 2-4 weeks with fever, headache, and high intracranial pressure. The presentation is often subtle with not all symptoms appearing as textbook descriptions. CT/MRI head typically shows no focal lesions.

Diagnosis options include: (1) Routine CSF analysis with India ink staining (rapid and inexpensive); (2) CSF and blood culture; (3) Blood serology; (4) Specimens from other sites such as skin lesions.

Acute phase therapy (Weeks 1-2): Amphotericin B 0.7-1 mg/kg per day IV drip over 4-6 hours in 250-500 ml D5% + Fluconazole 800 mg per day orally. Weeks 3-10: Fluconazole 800 mg/day orally. If amphotericin B is unavailable, fluconazole alone 800-2000 mg/day for 12 weeks. Maintenance phase: Fluconazole 200 mg/day until CD4 >200.

expanded_sections.heading: Abses Serebri

content_blocks.text: Brain abscess clinically resembles other intracranial space-occupying lesions. The evolution progresses through four stages. Early cerebritis (days 1-3): hypodense area with surrounding partial contrast enhancement. Late cerebritis (days 4-9): ring enhancement around the hypodense center becoming more complete. Early capsule formation (days 10-13): necrotic center shrinks, capsule thickens. Late capsule formation (after day 14): capsule becomes increasingly well-defined and thick.

Once an abscess has formed, surgical excision or drainage combined with prolonged antibiotics (usually 4-8 weeks) remains the treatment of choice. Definitive therapy targets the cultured organism from biopsy or primary infection focus.

expanded_sections.heading: Meningitis Bakterialis dan Ensefalitis Viral

content_blocks.text: Bacterial meningitis presents with the classic triad: fever, neck stiffness, and altered consciousness. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be broad-spectrum and initiated immediately after microbiological sampling. Definitive therapy is guided by culture results showing the identified organism and its antibiotic sensitivity/resistance patterns.

Viral encephalitis requires differentiated management based on immune status. In immunocompromised patients, look for CMV retinitis and perform LP PCR for HSV and VZV. In immunocompetent patients, perform LP PCR for CMV and examine skin/genital lesions. HSV typically involves the temporal lobes (limbic system); VZV affects the basal ganglia.

content_blocks.text: The general management of CNS infections follows a structured approach: (1) Handle emergencies including increased ICP with antiedema therapy, vital signs management with antipyretics and oxygenation, and metabolic correction via NGT; (2) Identify the causative microorganism through empirical clinical diagnosis and definitive testing including CSF analysis, neuroimaging, and other supportive investigations.

surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: Movement disorders are neurological symptoms characterized by abnormal voluntary movement and postural dysfunction, not caused by weakness from abnormal muscle tone. They are divided into two main categories: hyperkinetic (excessive movement) and hypokinetic (reduced movement). Prevalence of conditions like Parkinson disease, tremor, tics, and dystonia is approximately 1% in the population aged 65-85 years, increasing to 4.3% above age 85.

surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: Non-motor complications of Parkinson disease are organized into four categories. First, neuropsychiatric: depression (major, minor, dysthymia) treated with TCAs, SSRIs, or pramipexole; psychosis (hallucinations, loss of insight, delusions) managed by reducing dopaminergic therapy and avoiding polypharmacy; anxiety; cognitive impairment and dementia treated with rivastigmine and cholinesterase inhibitors. Second, autonomic dysfunction: cardiovascular orthostatic hypotension (fluids, elastic stockings), gastrointestinal issues (dysphagia, constipation, sialorrhea), urinary and sexual dysfunction. Third, sensory disturbances: pain (musculoskeletal, dystonic, neuropathic) managed by optimizing dopaminergic therapy; hyposmia as an early screening marker. Fourth, sleep disorders: insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness.

These are not caused by weakness due to abnormal muscle tone. The clinical picture is highly complex, variable, and sometimes unusual. Diagnosis can be challenging but is achievable through careful clinical examination.

expanded_sections.heading: Penyakit Parkinson
expanded_sections.subheading: Parkinson Disease - Definition and Cardinal Features

content_blocks.text: Parkinson disease is a form of parkinsonism characterized by degeneration of the substantia nigra pars compacta. Parkinsonism is a syndrome marked by resting tremor, rigidity, bradikinesia, and loss of postural reflexes due to dopamine deficiency.

The four cardinal symptoms (TRAP) are: Tremor, Rigiditas, Akinesia/Bradikinesia, and Postural reflex impairment. Items 1-3 are called the three cardinal signs. Presentation may be unilateral or bilateral, symmetric or asymmetric.

tables.title: Stadium PD menurut Hoehn dan Yahr
rows: Gejala bilateral, kecacatan minimal, gait terganggu
Gerak tubuh melambat, keseimbangan terganggu, disfungsi umum sedang
Gejala berat, berjalan terbatas, rigiditas bradikinesia
Stadium kahektik, kecacatan total, tidak mampu berdiri

bullets: Gejala kardinal: Tremor, Rigiditas, Akinesia/Bradikinesia, Postural reflex berkurang
Klasifikasi: Parkinsonisme idiopatik (primer), simptomatik (sekunder), Parkinson plus (multiple system degeneration), Heredodegeneratif

callouts.text: Postural instability typically appears in Hoehn-Yahr stage III and beyond; it is a late feature, not an early sign

expanded_sections.heading: Terapi Farmakologis PD
expanded_sections.subheading: Pharmacotherapy Based on Age and Stage

content_blocks.text: Pharmacological therapy is tailored to patient age, disease stage, side effect profile, and cost considerations. Long-term L-dopa use causes motor complications.

tables.title: Rekomendasi Terapi Berdasarkan Usia
rows: L-Dopa, kemudian ditambahkan DA agonist dan pramipexol

callouts.text: Long-term L-dopa causes motoric complications; younger patients may benefit from starting with DA agonists

content_blocks.text: NON-MOTOR COMPLICATIONS: Neuropsychiatric - depression (TCAs, SSRIs, pramipexole), psychosis (reduce dopaminergic therapy, avoid polypharmacy), anxiety, cognitive impairment/dementia (rivastigmine, cholinesterase inhibitors). Autonomic - orthostatic hypotension (fluids, elastic stockings, ephedrine 15-45mg/day, fludrocortisone 100-300mcg/day, midodrine 2.5-10mg/day), GI dysfunction (dysphagia, constipation, sialorrhea), urinary dysfunction (oxybutynin, desmopressin), sexual dysfunction. Sensory - pain (optimize dopaminergic therapy, botox), hyposmia. Sleep - insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness.

MOTOR COMPLICATIONS: Fluctuations - wearing off (short L-dopa effect), on-off phenomena. Dyskinesia - ballismus, dystonia. Management includes L-dopa dose adjustment, COMT inhibitors (entacapone) + L-dopa, pramipexole, ropinirole.

callouts.text: Motor fluctuations and dyskinesias are hallmarks of advanced PD and long-term L-dopa therapy

expanded_sections.heading: Parkinsonisme Sekunder dan MSA
expanded_sections.subheading: Secondary Parkinsonism and Multiple System Atrophy

content_blocks.text: Secondary parkinsonism resembles PD but has known causes including drug exposure, toxins, or structural lesions. Management includes removing the causative agent. Parkinson-plus syndromes include corticobasal degeneration, dementia syndromes, multiple system atrophy (MSA), and progressive supranuclear palsy.

MSA is a degenerative disease resembling parkinsonism with cerebellar signs and autonomic dysfunction. MSA-P (parkinsonism-dominant): incontinence, erectile dysfunction. MSA-C (cerebellar-dominant): nystagmus, dysarthria, ataxia. Red flags (MSA features): postural instability, orofacial dystonia, incontinence, myoclonic tremor, stridor and sigh inspiration, pyramidal signs. Probable MSA: age >30, urinary incontinence + orthostatic hypotension, responds to levodopa.

bullets: MSA-P (dominan parkinsonism): inkontinensia, disfungsi ereksi
MSA-C (dominan tanda serebelar): nistagmus, disartria, ataksia
Terapi: Levodopa untuk parkinsonism; hipotensi ortostatik (head up tilt, diet tinggi garam, elastic stocking, efedrin, fludrocortison, midodrine)
Disfungsi urinary: Oxybutynin dan Desmopresin spray

expanded_sections.heading: Tremor dan Distonia

content_blocks.text: Tremor is defined as rhythmic oscillatory movement from alternating agonist-antagonist muscle contraction. Classification includes resting tremor, action tremor (postural, kinetic, intentional, simple kinetic). Essential tremor is bilateral, affects hands and head, onset in second decade, usually starts unilateral then becomes bilateral.

Tremor treatment: propranolol 60-80mg/day (start 30mg), primidone 62.5-300mg/day, gabapentin 900-1800mg/day, clozapine 12.5-50mg/day, clonazepam 0.5-6mg/day. Cerebellar tremor is typically difficult to treat (carbamazepine, clonazepam, ondansetron may help).

Dystonia shows hypotonia with alternating muscle spasms, twisted postures, and potential body deformity. Classified as primary (idiopathic), secondary, and dystonia-plus. Treatment: levodopa, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics. Botulinum toxin injection 40-400 units for focal dystonias. Blepharospasm (M:F = 1:3) treated with botulinum toxin. Writer's cramp: involuntary finger contractions treated with physiotherapy and trihexyphenidyl.

bullets: Tremor esensial: bilateral tangan dan kepala, onset dekade kedua
Propranolol 60-80mg/hari (dimulai 30mg/hari)
Distonia: levodopa, agonis dopamin, antikolinergik, toksin botulinum

expanded_sections.heading: Tics, RLS, PLMD, dan Spasme Hemifasial

content_blocks.text: Tics are unconscious, brief, frequent, repetitive movements or sounds. Classification: Tourette syndrome (motor + vocal tics), chronic motor or vocal tic disorder, transient tic disorder (>4 weeks). Etiology involves biochemical imbalance in basal ganglia. Diagnosis uses MRI and EEG to rule out structural lesions. Treatment: non-neuroleptics (fluoxetine, paroxetine, clonidine) and neuroleptics (haloperidol, risperidone, clozapine).

Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) is a sensory-motor phenomenon with urge to move legs and unpleasant sensations. Classified as primary (genetic) or secondary (iron deficiency). By symptom pattern: intermittent, daily, or refractory. Clinical features: urge to move legs, worse in evening/night, causes sleep disruption, depression, usually family history, responds to dopaminergic therapy. Treatment goals: symptom reduction and secondary cause treatment. Non-pharmacological: mental activity, physical activity, sleep hygiene. Pharmacological: levodopa, dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, pergolide), anticonvulsants, opioids for refractory cases.

Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD) involves repetitive leg jerks during sleep every ~40 seconds, 0.5-5 seconds in duration, occurring every 20-40 seconds. Diagnosed by overnight polysomnography. Treatment: benzodiazepines (clonazepam), dopaminergics (pramipexole), anticonvulsants, GABA agonists (baclofen).

Hemifacial spasm involves unilateral tonic or clonic contractions of facial muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). Treatment aims to reduce muscle contraction: carbamazepine, benzodiazepines, baclofen, gabapentin, botulinum toxin injection, or surgery.

RLS: agonis dopamin (pramipexol, ropinirol, pergalide), levodopa, antikonvulsan, opioid
PLMD: klonazepam, pramipexole, antikonvulsan, baklofen
Spasme hemifasial: karbamazepin, benzodiazepin, baklofen, gabapentin, toksin botulinum, pembedahan

surgical_translation.clean_teaching_text: The brain is protected by bone, dura mater, and the blood-brain barrier. Uniquely, the brain lacks lymphatic vessels. Organisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites can reach the CNS via hematogenous spread, direct extension from sinus or mastoid infections, or penetrating trauma. Infection can affect multiple compartments: brain parenchyma, extra-axial spaces, or meninges. When treatment is inadequate, infection spreads to adjacent compartments. expanded_sections.heading: CNS Protection and Routes of Infection

content_blocks.text: The CNS is protected by multiple physical and physiological barriers: the bony skull and vertebral column, the dura mater, and the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Notably, the brain lacks a conventional lymphatic drainage system. Pathogens can reach the CNS through hematogenous spread (most common), direct extension from adjacent infected structures (sinus, mastoid), or penetrating trauma. When infection establishes, it can involve brain parenchyma (cerebritis, abscess, encephalitis), extra-axial spaces (subdural empyema, epidural abscess), or meninges (meningitis).

Ekstensi langsung dari sinus/mastoid
Trauma penetrasi

expanded_sections.heading: Cerebritis dan Formasi Kapsul

content_blocks.text: CEREBRITIS (7-10 days): The initial stage of pyogenic infection marked by edema with flattened gyri. Lesions may be bilateral in temporal and frontal regions depending on the area affected. CAPSULE FORMATION (10-14 days): As the infection matures, necrosis, debris, and pus accumulate in a central cavity. Granulation tissue and fibrocollagenous thickening form the abscess wall. Reactive astrocytosis, neovascularity, and vasogenic edema develop around the abscess. Blood supply becomes 3-5 times greater in gray matter compared to white matter in the affected area. Otogenic abscesses typically occur in the temporal lobe; rhinogenic abscesses in the frontal lobe.

bullets: Cerebritis: stadium awal infeksi piogenik (7-10 hari), edema, gyri mendatar
Capsul formasi: 10-14 hari setelah inokulasi, nekrosis, debris, pus
Granulasi dan penebalan dinding fibrokologen
Otogenik abses: lobus temporal; Rinogenik abses: lobus frontal

callouts.text: Temporal evolution is key: cerebritis 7-10 days, capsule formation begins at 10-14 days

expanded_sections.heading: Ensefalitis - CT dan MRI

content_blocks.text: Encephalitis is typically viral, causing acute, subacute, or chronic parenchymal inflammation. CT findings include vasogenic edema, mass effect, and heterogeneous enhancement with variable degrees. In later phases, mild hemorrhage may be visible. MRI is the modality of choice. T1W shows edema in affected areas; if complex with subacute hemorrhage, hyperintense areas may be seen. T1 C+ (gadolinium): enhancement is typically absent in early cases; in advanced cases, patterns include gyral enhancement, leptomeningeal enhancement, ring enhancement, and diffuse enhancement. T2W shows hyperintensity in white matter and cortex; hemorrhagic components appear hyperintense. DWI/ADC is more sensitive than T2WI - restricted diffusion occurs due to cytotoxic edema but is less intense than infarction. T2 shine-through can occur from vasogenic edema. GRE/SWI can demonstrate active hemorrhage (rare in neonates, common in older patients).

bullets: CT: vasogenic edema, efek massa, penyangatan heterogen
MRI T1: edema area terkena; T1 C+: gyral, leptomeningeal, ring, atau diffuse enhancement
MRI T2: hyperintensity white matter dan cortex
DWI/ADC: restricted diffusion (cytotoxic edema), lebih sensitif dari T2WI
GRE/SWI: dapat menunjukkan perdarahan aktif

callouts.text: DWI is more sensitive than T2 for early encephalitis; restricted diffusion from cytotoxic edema

expanded_sections.heading: Meningitis dan Empyema

content_blocks.text: MENINGITIS: Acute purulent meningitis shows exudate in the subarachnoid space, congested subarachnoid vessels, and brain swelling. Chronic forms are often due to TB or Cryptococcus. Complications include communicating hydrocephalus, ventriculitis, and dural vein thrombosis leading to infarction. EMPYEMA: Accumulation of inflammatory debris in the subdural space (rarely epidural).

bullets: Meningitis akut: eksudat di subarachnoid space, pembuluh darah kongesti, otak membengkak
Kronik: sering TB atau Kriptokokus

TOXOPLASMOSIS: CT shows multiple hypodense lesions with calcifications. With contrast: nodules and ring enhancement. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions on T2W.

expanded_sections.heading: Definisi dan Patofisiologi Infark Serebri

content_blocks.text: Cerebral infarction results from circulatory deficit due to thrombosis or cerebral embolism, manifesting as stroke. Predisposing factors include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, family history, and various conditions causing embolic or atherosclerotic disease. Symptoms may present as TIA (transient ischemic attack) with focal neurological deficits recovering within 24 hours, or as stroke with persistent neurological deficit.

bullets: Faktor predisposisi: Hipertensi, DM, riwayat keluarga
Gejala: TIA (defisit neurologis fokal recovery dalam 24 jam) atau Stroke (defisit persisten)

expanded_sections.heading: Gambaran Radiologi Infark
expanded_sections.subheading: CT and MRI Findings in Cerebral Infarction

content_blocks.text: CT FINDINGS: CT may be normal in very early infarction and typically becomes clearly apparent after 24 hours. Early signs include loss of gray-white matter differentiation in the affected area and hypodense lesions in the vascular territory involved. HYPERDENSE MCA SIGN: On non-contrast CT, a hyperdense middle cerebral artery indicates acute thrombus within the vessel, an important early sign of large vessel occlusion. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) shows restricted diffusion within minutes of ischemia onset.

expanded_sections.heading: Definisi dan Prinsip Rehabilitasi

content_blocks.text: Rehabilitation is a dynamic process to help a person achieve optimal physical, emotional, psychological, social, and vocational potential while maintaining dignity and self-respect. Neurorehabilitation specifically aims to aid recovery from nervous system injury and minimize or compensate for functional alterations. Rehabilitation should begin at initial patient contact.

GOALS: Restore patient to independence or regain pre-illness status; maximize independence within disability limits; realize goals based on individual assessment; active patient participation; facilitate activities of daily living (ADL); motivate patient toward social independence.

TYPES: Medical rehabilitation (restoration of structure and function); Vocational rehabilitation (restoration of earning capacity); Social rehabilitation (restoration of family and social relationships); Psychological rehabilitation (restoration of personal dignity and confidence). APPROACHES: Institution-based, outreach-based, community-based (Rehabilitasi Berbasis Masyarakat).

bullets: Physical independence
Mobility
Social integration
Occupational integration

expanded_sections.heading: Tim Rehabilitasi Neuro

content_blocks.text: The neurorehabilitation team is multidisciplinary. Physicians include physiatrist, orthopedic surgeon, neurologist, neurosurgeon, psychiatrist, and pediatrician. Paramedical members include physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech pathologist, rehabilitation nurse, psychologist, social worker, and vocational counselor.

bullets: Medical team: Physiatrist, Orthopaedic surgeon, Neurologist, Neurosurgeon, Plastic surgeon, Psychiatrist, Paediatrician
Paramedical: Physiotherapist, Occupational therapist, Rehabilitation nurse, Speech pathologist, Psychologist, Social worker
Others: Prosthetist, Recreation therapist, Vocational counsellor, Family members, Community, NGO

expanded_sections.heading: Positioning dan Transfer

content_blocks.text: POSITIONING prevents musculoskeletal deformities, contractures, ankylosis, pressure ulcers, decreased vascular supply, thrombosis, and edema. The unconscious patient should be repositioned every 2 hours. Spastic patients require frequent repositioning. Use pillows for body alignment, trochanter rolls, and positioning devices. For weak or paralyzed arms, position to approximate glenoid cavity; use axillary pillow to prevent adduction. For feet, use high-top sneakers or splints to prevent foot drop and pressure ulcers.

TRANSFER TYPES: Two-person lift (no active patient participation); Mechanical lift (lifting device); Contact guard (verbal cues + minimal physical support); Supervision (verbal cues only). Key principles: transfer toward unaffected side; properly fitted flat shoes; never pull on paretic arm; stand on affected side if balance is unsteady; use knee-to-knee block if knees buckle.

HEMIPLEGIC BED-TO-SIT TRANSFER: Move to side of bed; slip unaffected leg under affected leg as transfer cradle; place affected arm on abdomen; push off mattress with unaffected elbow while turning hips; swing unaffected leg over bed edge; push up with unaffected hand; lean on unaffected hand to maintain erect position.

bullets: Reposisi pasien tak sadar tiap 2 jam
Transfer ke sisi tak terkena
Jangan menarik lengan paretil
Walker atau four-point cane untuk support

callouts.text: Never pull on the paretic arm during transfers - this causes shoulder subluxation and pain

expanded_sections.heading: Fisioterapi Modalitas

content_blocks.text: HEAT THERAPY: Increases blood flow and connective tissue extensibility; decreases joint stiffness, pain, and muscle spasm; reduces inflammation. Types: hot pack, infrared ray, paraffin bath (49 degrees C), hydrotherapy (warm water), diathermy. INDICATIONS: sprains, myositis, arthralgia, neuralgia, muscle spasm, strains. COLD THERAPY: Reduces inflammation, edema, and exudates. ELECTRICAL STIMULATION: For denervated or involuntarily innervated muscle to prevent disuse atrophy and spasticity. TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) for chronic low back pain, neuralgia, contusion. TRACTION: For extrinsic muscle spasm, HNP, cervical/lumbar traction. MASSAGE and BIOFEEDBACK (EMG, galvanic skin response).

bullets: Heat: hot pack, infrared, paraffin bath 49C, hydrotherapy, diathermy
Cold: reduce inflammation and edema
TENS: chronic low back pain, neuralgia, contusion
Traction: cervical, lumbar for HNP

expanded_sections.heading: Bobath NDT dan Disfagia

content_blocks.text: BOBATH/NDT APPROACH: Used for hemiplegia from stroke, brain injury, and cerebral palsy. Major goal is normalization of muscle tone, posture, movement, and function. Reintegration of both body sides. Proximal-to-distal positioning, weight bearing on affected side, symmetric midline starting position, movement toward affected side encouraged. Straighten trunk and neck to promote symmetry and normalize tone. Position hemiplegic patients opposite to spastic patterns: avoid flexion/adduction in upper extremity and extension in lower extremity.

DYSPHAGIA ASSESSMENT (Simple bedside test): Position patient upright; give 1 teaspoon (5ml) cold water with head slightly flexed; check lip closure during swallow; palpate larynx for elevation; monitor for delayed or incomplete swallow; have patient vocalize 'aaaa' - monitor for wet/hoarse voice; have patient cough and repeat vocalization. If patient cannot swallow or voice becomes wet -> NGT insertion required. Feeding position: upright 90 degrees, head flexed forward, chin tucked, small bites, thorough chewing.

Disfagia: beri 1 sdt air dingin, palpasi elevasi laring, suara 'aaaa'
Posisi makan: tegak 90 derajat, dagu tuck, suapan kecil

callouts.text: Wet voice after swallowing indicates aspiration - NGT may be needed

expanded_sections.heading: Manajemen Bladder dan Bowel

content_blocks.text: BLADDER MANAGEMENT: Four categories of urinary incontinence: urge (abrupt strong desire to void), stress (loss with coughing/sneezing), overflow (overdistension), functional (factors outside lower urinary tract). Bladder training: education, scheduled voiding (initial interval 2-3 hours), positive reinforcement. Prompted voiding for cognitively impaired: regular monitoring, prompting to use bathroom, praising continence. Pelvic muscle (Kegel) exercises: contract to count of 10, relax to count of 10, 50-100 daily, improvement in 4-6 weeks. Bladder-triggering techniques: suprapubic stimulation, Valsalva maneuver, Crede maneuver.

BOWEL MANAGEMENT: Constipation causes: fluid restriction, immobility, decreased bulk, constipating drugs (codeine), spinal compression, paralytic ileus. Bowel training: ensure lower bowel empty (enema if needed), establish regular timing based on previous pattern, high roughage diet, increase fluid to 2000-2500 mL/day, suppository on first day, seated position for defecation.

Kegel: kontraksi 10 detik, relaksasi 10 detik, 50-100x/hari
Bowel training: serat tinggi, cairan 2000-2500 ml/hari

content_blocks.text: STROKE REHABILITATION: Goals - optimize recovery, modify residual symptoms, achieve independent functional activity, environmental adaptation, quality of life. Three phases: Acute (first 2 weeks, hemodynamic stabilization, prevent complications); Subacute (2 weeks-6 months, restore ADL, walking, life roles); Chronic (>6 months, endurance and muscle strengthening). Principles: maximize movement, functional movement goals, sitting and standing stability, 45-60 minute sessions, cognitive function support. Complications of prolonged bed rest: cardiovascular (DVT risk, orthostatic hypotension), respiratory (retention, pneumonia), musculoskeletal (weakness, contracture, osteoporosis), metabolic (decreased glucose tolerance), integumentary (pressure ulcers), GI (constipation), GU (urinary incontinence), CNS (decreased cognition).

BRAIN INJURY: Positioning, supportive eating and standing, motor control rehabilitation, bowel/bladder care, pain management, balance training, memory aids. SPINAL CORD INJURY: Safe transportation, traction, positioning, active/passive ROM, mat work, orthoses, gait training, mobility training. PARKINSONISM: Reduce rigidity and maintain flexibility, balance training, coordination exercises, breathing and chest expansion exercises.

expanded_sections.heading: Definisi dan Klasifikasi

content_blocks.text: An epileptic seizure is the transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain (ILAE). The ILAE 2017 classification organizes epilepsies by seizure type: Focal Onset (seizures originating in one hemisphere, with or without impaired awareness), Generalized Onset (seizures involving both hemispheres from onset, including motor and non-motor types), and Unknown Onset (when onset cannot be determined).

expanded_sections.heading: Klasifikasi Tipe Bangkitan

content_blocks.text: Seizures are classified by their pattern of onset and clinical manifestations. Focal seizures may spread to become bilateral tonic-clonic. Awareness (previously called consciousness) is a key distinguishing feature within focal seizures. Generalized seizures include tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic, and atonic types.

expanded_sections.heading: Bangkitan Refleks dan Pemeriksaan Penunjang

content_blocks.text: Reflex seizures are triggered by specific stimuli including visual (flashing lights, patterns), auditory, somatosensory, and somatomotor triggers. Ancillary testing for epilepsy evaluation includes neuroimaging (CT/MRI), laboratory tests, CSF analysis, EEG, and EKG (to rule out cardiac causes of syncope).

expanded_sections.heading: Kelainan Kongenital

content_blocks.text: CHORISTOMA: Normal tissue growing in an abnormal location. Can be found throughout the body. Example: Leptomeningeal rhabdomyomatosis - striated muscle elements in the cerebellopontine angle region. CYST: Lesion formed as a sac from membranous tissue containing fluid, air, semisolid material, or other substances. CNS cysts include: Colloid cyst (contains colloid fluid), Epidermoid cyst (lined by flattened squamous cells, may contain keratin mass), Arachnoid cyst (contains CSF accumulation).

bullets: Choristoma: jaringan normal di lokasi abnormal

expanded_sections.heading: Penyakit Serebrovaskular

content_blocks.text: INFARK SEREBRI: Brain tissue death caused by disrupted blood flow. Lesions are irreversible; brain cells undergo necrosis. ANEURYSMA INTRAKRANIAL: Dilation or protrusion of cerebral blood vessels due to weakened vessel wall, also called saccular or berry aneurysm. Predominantly located at the Circle of Willis. MALFORMASI VASKULAR: Abnormal vascular connections. EPIDURAL HEMATOMA: Blood collection between skull and dura. SUBDURAL HEMATOMA: Blood collection between dura and arachnoid.

bullets: Infark serebri: kematian jaringan otak akibat gangguan aliran darah, irreversible
Aneurysma intracranial: pelebaran pembuluh darah otak, predominant di Circle of Willis
Epidural hematoma: di antara tulang dan duramater
Subdural hematoma: di antara duramater dan arakhnoid

expanded_sections.heading: Penyakit Infeksi

content_blocks.text: DEMYELINATING DISEASE: Loss of myelin sheath causing nerve signal disruption; can form demyelinating pseudotumor lesions. BACTERIAL INFECTION: Brain abscess - microscopically shows purulent necrotic mass bordered by brain parenchyma; etiology includes Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Clostridium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. FUNGAL INFECTION (Mycoses): Cryptococcoma; etiology includes Aspergillus, Candida, Histoplasma. PARASITIC INFECTION: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium larva in pork); Toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii from cat feces) - microscopically shows minute basophilic structures containing parasites with surrounding lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. VIRAL INFECTION: Herpes Simplex encephalitis, Varicella-zoster virus, HIV.

bullets: Abses otak: Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Clostridium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis

expanded_sections.heading: Tumor - Astrositoma

content_blocks.text: Astrocytoma is a brain tumor arising from astrocytes. Highly variable depending on location in the CNS, potentially invasive and progressive. Most cases are intracranial; only ~3% are intraspinal. Can occur at all ages, average 35-40 years. Well-differentiated astrocytomas tend to occur in younger patients; anaplastic types more common in middle age. In adults, slightly more common in males. Cerebral hemisphere predilection; in children more commonly in cerebellum. Clinical features depend on location and growth rate. Combination of increased intracranial pressure, progressive neurological deficits, seizures, and cognitive decline is commonly seen. WHO CLASSIFICATION: Grade I (pilocytic astrocytoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma); Grade II (diffuse astrocytoma, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, pilomyxoid astrocytoma); Grade III (anaplastic astrocytoma); Grade IV (glioblastoma multiforme). Grade is still best determined by mitotic count.

bullets: WHO Grade I: Pilocytic astrocytoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
WHO Grade II: Diffuse astrocytoma, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, pilomyxoid astrocytoma
WHO Grade III: Anaplastic astrocytoma
WHO Grade IV: Glioblastoma multiforme
Grade terbaik tetap berdasarkan jumlah mitosis

callouts.text: Glioblastoma multiforme = WHO Grade IV, most malignant astrocytic tumor

expanded_sections.heading: Oligodendroglioma dan Meningioma

content_blocks.text: OLIGODENDROGLIOMA: Arises from oligodendrocytes. Can be low-grade (WHO Grade II) or high-grade (WHO Grade III/anaplastic). Commonly found in frontal and temporal lobes. Grossly soft, grayish-pink. Contains mineral deposits (calcifications), hemorrhage, and/or cysts. Histology: small round monotonous nuclei, perinuclear halos ('fried egg' appearance), branching thin-walled vessels ('chicken-wire' vessels), microcalcifications (calcospherites). Typically slow-growing, present for years before diagnosis.

MENINGIOMA: Arises from meningothelial cells of the protective meninges. Most common benign brain tumor, slow-growing, usually intracranial but can occur in spinal cord. More common in females, especially adults. Hormonal influence: progesterone receptor expression; tumor size changes during luteal phase and pregnancy. 40-80% have abnormal chromosome 22 at NF2 locus. NF2 is a tumor suppressor gene at 22q12. WHO 2016 classification: Grade I (benign), Grade II (atypical), Grade III (anaplastic). Key histological types: meningepithelial (syncytial), fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous.

expanded_sections.heading: Manajemen Pasca Stroke

content_blocks.text: Post-stroke management requires differentiating between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke as management pathways diverge significantly. Key management domains include blood pressure control, prevention of complications, early mobilization, and secondary prevention.

content_blocks.text: ISCHEMIC STROKE: BP management follows permissive hypertension principles unless >220/120 mmHg or specific indications exist. Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel) for secondary prevention. Statins for atherosclerotic disease. Avoid anticoagulation in acute phase. HEMORRHAGIC STROKE: Aggressive BP lowering (target <140/90). Reverse anticoagulation if present. Neurosurgical consultation for cerebellar hematoma >3cm, hydrocephalus, or clinical deterioration. ICP management with osmotherapy.

expanded_sections.heading: Komplikasi dan Perawatan Keperawatan

content_blocks.text: Common post-stroke complications include deep vein thrombosis (DVT), aspiration pneumonia, pressure sores (decubitus), joint contractures, spasticity, depression, shoulder subluxation, and nutritional deficiencies. Nursing care includes proper positioning every 2 hours, range of motion (ROM) exercises, joint mobilization, and contracture prevention. Physical therapy should begin as early as medically feasible.

Latihan ROM aktif dan pasif
Mobilisasi sendi

content_blocks.text: DYSPHAGIA ASSESSMENT: All stroke patients must have swallowing assessment before any oral intake. Bedside water swallow test: give 1 teaspoon of cold water, observe for coughing, wet voice, or delayed swallow. If failed, NGT feeding is required. NUTRITION: Enteral nutrition via NGT if dysphagia present. Target 25-30 kcal/kg/day. Monitor for aspiration. BOWEL MANAGEMENT: Prevent constipation with adequate hydration, fiber, and regular bowel regimen. BLADDER MANAGEMENT: Assess for urinary retention; intermittent catheterization if needed; avoid indwelling catheter if possible.

Nutrisi enteral: 25-30 kkal/kgBB/hari
Pencegahan konstipasi: hidrasi, serat, regimen teratur
Manajemen kandung kemih: katerisasi intermiten, hindari kater permanen

callouts.text: Never give oral intake before swallowing assessment - aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in stroke patients

content_blocks.text: Coma management follows Brain Trauma Foundation (BTF) guidelines. HEAD POSITIONING: Elevate head of bed 30 degrees. Keep head midline to optimize cerebral venous drainage. Avoid neck flexion or rotation. ICP MONITORING: Maintain ICP <20 mmHg. CPP (Cerebral Perfusion Pressure) should be maintained at 60-70 mmHg. Calculate as MAP - ICP. SEDATION: Use propofol or midazolam for ICP control. Avoid hypotension. OSMOTHERAPY: Mannitol 0.25-1 g/kg IV or hypertonic saline 3% for elevated ICP. SEIZURE PROPHYLAXIS: Phenytoin or levetiracetam for first 7 days post-TBI. GLUCOSE MANAGEMENT: Maintain normoglycemia (80-180 mg/dL). TEMPERATURE: Prevent fever; treat aggressively if present.

callouts.text: CPP = MAP - ICP; maintaining CPP 60-70 mmHg is critical to prevent secondary brain injury

Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes TB meningitis with characteristic basilar enhancement

content_blocks.text: The most common pyogenic bacteria causing CNS infection are Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common in adults), Neisseria meningitidis (young adults, epidemics), and Haemophilus influenzae (children, now decreased due to vaccination). Other pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus (post-traumatic, post-neurosurgical), Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B strep, neonates), and Listeria monocytogenes (immunocompromised, elderly, pregnant women).

expanded_sections.heading: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

content_blocks.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes TB meningitis, typically through hematogenous spread from pulmonary TB or rupture of subependymal tubercles (Rich foci) into the subarachnoid space. Characteristic basilar meningeal enhancement on imaging. Treatment requires prolonged OAT regimen (9-12 months) with good BBB penetration (pyrazinamide, isoniazid).

bullets: Menyebar hematogen dari TB paru
Rupture fokus Rich subependymal
Enhancement basal meningeal khas
OAT 9-12 bulan

content_blocks.text: CRYPTOCOCCUS NEOFORMANS: Most common fungal CNS pathogen in immunocompromised (especially HIV/AIDS). Found in pigeon droppings/soil. Thick polysaccharide capsule visible with India ink. AS PERGILLUS: Angioinvasive, causes hemorrhagic infarction. Risk factors: neutropenia, transplant recipients. CANDIDA: Candida albicans most common; causes meningitis, abscess, microabscesses. Risk factors: immunocompromised, long-term catheterization.

PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM: Causes cerebral malaria through sequestration of parasitized RBCs in cerebral microvasculature. ENTAMOEBA HISTOLYTICA: Causes brain abscess. TAENIA SOLIUM (PORK TAPEWORM): Causes neurocysticercosis, most common parasitic CNS infection worldwide. Larval cysts in brain parenchyma, subarachnoid space, ventricles. Four stages: vesicular, colloidal, granular, calcified. NAEGLERIA FOWLERI: Free-living amoeba in warm freshwater; causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), almost universally fatal. TOXOPLASMA GONDII: Causes toxoplasmosis encephalitis in immunocompromised; ring-enhancing lesions, typically reactivation of latent infection.

callouts.text: Naegleria fowleri PAM has >95% mortality; diagnosis often post-mortem

content_blocks.text: HSV-1 (Herpes Simplex Virus type 1): Most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in the US. Characteristic temporal lobe involvement. Clinical features: fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures. CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, normal glucose. PCR is diagnostic. Treatment: acyclovir 10mg/kg IV q8h for 14-21 days. CMV (Cytomegalovirus): Causes ventriculoencephalitis in immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant). Periventricular enhancement. VZV (Varicella Zoster Virus): Can cause meningitis, encephalitis, vasculopathy, especially in elderly and immunocompromised. HIV: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND), aseptic meningitis, opportunistic infections. RABIES: Negri bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions) in neurons; almost universally fatal once symptomatic.

callouts.text: HSV encephalitis: temporal lobe involvement on MRI; PCR is gold standard; acyclovir should be started empirically if suspected

content_blocks.text: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord. The brain is divided into cerebrum (two cerebral hemispheres), cerebellum, and brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata). Understanding the anatomical relationships and vascular territories is essential for clinical localization.

Sistem saraf tepi

content_blocks.text: ANTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (ACA): Supplies medial frontal and parietal lobes, anterior corpus callosum, anterior limb of internal capsule, anterior fornix. Clinical deficit: contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, abulia, urinary incontinence. MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY (MCA): Supplies lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, posterior limb of internal capsule, basal ganglia. Clinical deficit: contralateral face/arm weakness and sensory loss > leg, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant hemisphere), hemianopia. POSTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (PCA): Supplies occipital lobe, medial temporal lobe, thalamus, midbrain. Clinical deficit: homonymous hemianopia, memory deficits, alexia without agraphia (dominant hemisphere).

expanded_sections.subheading: Internal Capsule Anatomy and Vascular Supply

content_blocks.text: The internal capsule is a white matter structure containing ascending and descending fiber tracts between the thalamus/caudate and lentiform nucleus. ANTERIOR LIMB: frontopontine fibers, thalamocortical fibers. GENU: corticobulbar fibers (face). POSTERIOR LIMB: corticospinal tract (face, arm, leg in somatotopic order), thalamocortical fibers. RETROLENTICULAR: optic radiations, corticopontine fibers. SUBLENTICULAR: auditory radiations. Vascular supply: lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) supply most of internal capsule. LACUNAR INFARCTS commonly affect the internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons. Pure motor hemiparesis from internal capsule lacune is the most common lacunar syndrome.

bullets: Lengan anterior: serat frontopontin, talamokortikal
Genu: serat kortikobulbar (wajah)

Retrolentikular: radiasi optik
Sublentikular: radiasi auditorik
Suplai: arteri lentikulostriata (cabang MCA)

callouts.text: Internal capsule lacune causes pure motor hemiparesis - face, arm, and leg equally affected

content_blocks.text: PARKINSONIAN GAIT: Shuffling steps, narrow base, flexed posture (stooped), reduced or absent arm swing, en bloc turning, festination (acceleration), difficulty initiating movement. HEMIPLEGIC GAIT: Circumduction of affected leg (swinging leg outward in arc), foot drop with toe dragging, extended knee on affected side, decreased weight bearing on affected leg, compensatory leaning. ATAXIC GAIT (Cerebellar): Wide-based, unsteady, veering toward affected side, positive Romberg. SPASTIC GAIT: Scissoring (adduction of legs), toe walking. STEPPAGE GAIT: From foot drop, excessive hip/knee flexion to clear foot. WADDLING GAIT: Bilateral hip girdle weakness, excessive trunk sway.

content_blocks.text: The brachial plexus is formed by C5-T1 nerve roots, divided into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal branches. UPPER TRUNK (C5-C6): injury causes Erb-Duchenne palsy - 'waiter's tip' deformity (adducted shoulder, internally rotated arm, extended elbow, flexed wrist). Common in birth injury (shoulder dystocia) and motorcycle accidents. LOWER TRUNK (C8-T1): injury causes Klumpke palsy - claw hand deformity, weakness of intrinsic hand muscles, possible Horner syndrome (if sympathetic chain involved). LONG THORACIC NERVE (C5-C7): innervates serratus anterior; injury causes winged scapula.

content_blocks.text: Headaches are classified into primary headaches (migraine, tension-type, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, other primary headaches) and secondary headaches (symptom of another condition). The ICHD-3 (International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition) provides standardized diagnostic criteria.

content_blocks.text: Migraine is characterized by recurrent headache attacks lasting 4-72 hours, typically unilateral, pulsating, moderate to severe intensity, aggravated by routine physical activity, and associated with nausea and/or photophobia and phonophobia. MIGRAINE WITH AURA: Recurrent attacks with fully reversible focal neurological symptoms (visual, sensory, speech) that develop gradually over 5-20 minutes and last less than 60 minutes. Visual aura is most common (scintillating scotoma, fortification spectra). MIGRAINE WITHOUT AURA: Most common type (~70-80%). CHRONIC MIGRAINE: Headache on >=15 days/month for >3 months, with migraine features on >=8 days/month.

callouts.text: P-O-U-N-D mnemonic for migraine: Pulsating, duration 4-72h, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling

content_blocks.text: The SNOOP4 mnemonic helps identify dangerous secondary headaches requiring urgent investigation. S - Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malignancy); N - Neurological signs or symptoms (focal deficit, seizure, papilledema); O - Onset sudden (thunderclap headache - SAH until proven otherwise); O - Older age (>50, especially with temporal artery tenderness - consider giant cell arteritis); P - Pattern change (progressive, different from usual); P - Precipitated by exertion/cough/sex; P - Positional (worse upright suggests CSF leak, worse supine suggests raised ICP); P - Progressive (worsening frequency/severity).

tables.title: SNOOP4 Red Flags
rows: Tumor, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, CSF leak

callouts.text: Thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise - immediate CT non-contrast, if negative consider LP for xanthochromia

content_blocks.text: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: The trigeminovascular system is central to migraine pathophysiology. Activation of trigeminal nerve fibers innervating meningeal blood vessels releases CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide), substance P, and neurokinin A, causing neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, and pain signal transmission. The brainstem (periaqueductal gray, locus coeruleus) and hypothalamus play modulatory roles. Cortical spreading depression (CSD) is the substrate for migraine aura.

ACUTE TREATMENT: Step 1 - NSAIDs/acetaminophen (mild attacks). Step 2 - Triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan) - 5-HT1B/1D agonists, first-line for moderate-severe attacks, contraindicated in cardiovascular disease. Step 3 - Anti-emetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) for nausea and enhancing absorption. Step 4 - Rescue medications (dexamethasone to prevent recurrence). ER protocol: IV metoclopramide + fluids.

callouts.text: Triptans are contraindicated in cardiovascular disease, hemiplegic migraine, and basilar migraine

content_blocks.text: INDICATIONS: >=4 migraine days/month, significant disability, frequent use of acute medications (>2 days/week), failure of acute treatment. OPTIONS: Beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol); CCBs (flunarizine); Antiepileptics (topiramate, valproate); Tricyclics (amitriptyline); CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab); Oral CGRP antagonists (rimegepant, atogepant); OnabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine.

Menentukan stadium PD menggunakan Hoehn-Yahr dan menerapkan terapi yang tepat
key_points: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra pars compacta causes striatal dopamine deficiency
Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein aggregates) are pathological hallmark
TRAP symptoms: Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural Instability
UK Brain Bank criteria: Bradykinesia + at least one of rigidity, rest tremor, postural instability
Levodopa remains gold standard; motor complications (wearing-off, dyskinesia) develop with long-term use

expanded_sections.heading: Epidemiologi

content_blocks.text: Parkinson disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer disease. Incidence increases with age, with peak onset between 55-65 years. Prevalence is approximately 1% of population over 60 years, rising to 4% over 80 years. Slightly more common in males than females. Mean age of onset is 60 years; onset before 40 years is considered young-onset PD; before 20 years is juvenile PD.

bullets: Penyakit neurodegeneratif kedua tersering setelah Alzheimer
Prevalensi: 1% populasi >60 tahun, 4% >80 tahun
Puncak onset: 55-65 tahun
Sedikit lebih sering pada laki-laki

expanded_sections.heading: Etiologi dan Patofisiologi

content_blocks.text: ETIOLOGY: Multifactorial - combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors. Genetic: 10-15% familial; mutations in SNCA (alpha-synuclein), LRRK2, PARK2 (parkin), PINK1, DJ-1. Environmental: pesticides, herbicides, solvents, head trauma, protective factors (smoking, coffee, uric acid). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra pars compacta (pars ventralis, lateral > medial) leads to dopamine deficiency in striatum. Disrupts direct (D1, excitatory) and indirect (D2, inhibitory) pathways, resulting in increased thalamic inhibition and reduced cortical excitation. By the time motor symptoms appear, 60-80% of nigral neurons and 80% of striatal dopamine are lost. LEWY BODIES: Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions containing aggregated alpha-synuclein; pathological hallmark. Found not only in substantia nigra but also cortex, autonomic ganglia, and peripheral nervous system. Braak staging describes spread: Stage 1-2 (dorsal motor nucleus of vagus), Stage 3-4 (substantia nigra), Stage 5-6 (cortex).

bullets: Degenerasi neuron dopaminergik substantia nigra pars compacta
60-80% neuron hilang saat gejala motorik muncul
Lewy bodies: alpha-synuclein aggregates
Braak staging: medulla -> substantia nigra -> korteks

callouts.text: 80% striatal dopamine loss before symptoms appear - enormous functional reserve

content_blocks.text: The four cardinal motor symptoms (TRAP) are: TREMOR AT REST: Most common initial symptom (70%); starts unilateral, typically in one hand; pill-rolling motion (4-6 Hz); decreases with action, increases with stress and walking; may involve jaw, tongue, legs. RIGIDITY: Increased resistance to passive movement throughout range; cogwheel (with tremor) or lead-pipe (without tremor); affects all limbs and axial muscles. BRADYKINESIA/AKINESIA: Slowness of movement and decrement in amplitude; difficulty initiating movement; reduced facial expression (masked facies/hypomimia), micrographia, decreased blink rate. POSTURAL INSTABILITY: Loss of postural reflexes; appears later (Hoehn-Yahr Stage 3+); not present in early PD - if present early, consider atypical parkinsonism. NON-MOTOR SYMPTOMS: Cognitive impairment/dementia (30-40%), depression (40%), anxiety, apathy, autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary dysfunction), REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, constipation (often precedes motor symptoms by years).

callouts.text: Postural instability is a LATE feature - if present early, think atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP)

content_blocks.text: UK BRAIN BANK CRITERIA: Step 1 - Diagnosis of Parkinson syndrome: Bradykinesia (slowness of initiation + reduced amplitude/speed) AND at least one of: muscular rigidity, 4-6 Hz rest tremor, postural instability (not caused by visual, vestibular, cerebellar, or proprioceptive dysfunction). Step 2 - Exclusion criteria (absence of features suggesting alternative diagnoses): history of repeated strokes, repeated head injury, encephalitis, neuroleptic use, more than one affected relative, strictly unilateral features after 3 years, supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early severe autonomic involvement, early severe dementia, Babinski sign, CT evidence of tumor or hydrocephalus. Step 3 - Supportive prospective positive criteria (three or more required for definite PD): unilateral onset, rest tremor, progressive disorder, persistent asymmetry, excellent response to levodopa, severe levodopa-induced chorea, clinical course >10 years. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Essential tremor (bilateral, action tremor, head involvement, no rigidity/bradykinesia); Drug-induced parkinsonism (neuroleptics, metoclopramide, reserpine); Vascular parkinsonism (lower body, stepwise progression, pyramidal signs); MSA (early autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, poor levodopa response); PSP (early falls, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity); Corticobasal degeneration (asymmetric, cortical signs, alien limb); Dementia with Lewy bodies (early dementia, visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition).

callouts.text: Excellent response to levodopa is a strong supportive criterion for idiopathic PD

content_blocks.text: HOEHN-YAHR STAGING: Stage 1 - Unilateral involvement, minimal/no functional impairment; Stage 2 - Bilateral involvement, no balance impairment; Stage 3 - Bilateral, mild to moderate postural instability, physically independent; Stage 4 - Severe disability, still able to walk/stand unassisted; Stage 5 - Wheelchair-bound or bedridden unless aided. PHARMACOLOGICAL MANAGEMENT: LEVODOPA (gold standard): combined with carbidopa or benserazide to prevent peripheral conversion; started at low dose, titrated up; best for symptomatic relief; motor complications (wearing-off, dyskinesia) develop with long-term use. DOPAMINE AGONISTS (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine): directly stimulate dopamine receptors; can be used as monotherapy in early disease or adjunct to levodopa; benefit: fewer motor complications; risk: impulse control disorders, somnolence, peripheral edema. MAO-B INHIBITORS (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide): reduce dopamine metabolism; mild symptomatic benefit; may have neuroprotective properties. COMT INHIBITORS (entacapone, tolcapone, opicapone): extend levodopa half-life; used as adjunct to reduce wearing-off. ANTICHOLINERGICS (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine): useful for tremor-predominant young patients; avoid in elderly (cognitive side effects). AMANTADINE: mild antiparkinsonian effect; useful for dyskinesia.

callouts.text: Levodopa remains gold standard; DA agonists as first-line in young to delay motor complications

expanded_sections.heading: Manajemen Non-Farmakologis dan DBS
expanded_sections.subheading: Non-Pharmacological Management and Deep Brain Stimulation

content_blocks.text: NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL: Physiotherapy (gait training, balance exercises, ROM); Occupational therapy (ADL adaptation); Speech therapy (dysarthria, dysphagia); Exercise programs (tai chi, dance, cycling); Nutritional management (protein redistribution diet to optimize levodopa absorption). DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION (DBS): Indications - motor fluctuations despite optimal medical therapy, dyskinesia limiting levodopa dose, tremor refractory to medication. Targets: STN (subthalamic nucleus) - allows medication reduction; GPi (globus pallidus interna) - directly reduces dyskinesia. Contraindications: dementia, severe depression, atypical parkinsonism, severe cerebrovascular disease. BEST CANDIDATES: Responsive to levodopa (>=30% improvement), no cognitive impairment, no active psychiatric disease, medically optimized.

Target: STN (reduksi obat), GPi (reduksi diskinisia)

Kandidat terbaik: respons L-dopa >=30%, tidak ada gangguan kognitif

modules.overview: Kuliah tentang patofisiologi stroke yang mencakup definisi, klasifikasi (iskemik vs hemoragik), faktor risiko (dapat dimodifikasi dan tidak dapat dimodifikasi), patofisiologi iskemia serebral (kaskade iskemik, eksitotoksisitas, konsep penumbra), neuroproteksi, prinsip manajemen akut, serta aspek nutrisi dalam perawatan stroke. Menyertakan kaskade iskemik dari oklusi pembuluh darah hingga kematian neuron dan konsep penumbra iskemik sebagai target intervensi akut.

key_points: Stroke is defined as rapidly developing clinical signs of focal cerebral disturbance lasting >24 hours or leading to death
Ischemic stroke (85%) results from thrombosis, embolism, or systemic hypoperfusion; Hemorrhagic stroke (15%) from intracerebral hemorrhage or SAH
Ischemic cascade: energy failure -> ion pump dysfunction -> glutamate release -> calcium influx -> free radical production -> inflammation -> cell death
Penumbra = tissue at risk around the infarct core; salvageable with prompt reperfusion
Golden hour: treatment within 4.5 hours for IV thrombolysis, up to 24 hours for selected mechanical thrombectomy

content_blocks.text: WHO definition: Rapidly developing clinical signs of focal (or global) disturbance of cerebral function, lasting more than 24 hours or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than of vascular origin. Stroke is classified into: ISCHEMIC STROKE (85% of all strokes) - from thrombosis, embolism, or systemic hypoperfusion; HEMORRHAGIC STROKE (15%) - intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK (TIA): focal neurological deficit resolving within 24 hours (traditional) or without tissue infarction on imaging (tissue-based definition).

NON-MODIFIABLE: Age (risk doubles each decade after 55), sex (men > women, but women have higher mortality), race (African Americans, Hispanics higher risk), family history, prior stroke/TIA. MODIFIABLE: Hypertension (most important modifiable risk factor), diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, smoking, dyslipidemia, obesity, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic syndrome. NUTRITIONAL RISK FACTORS: High sodium intake, low potassium intake, high saturated fat, low fruit/vegetable consumption, obesity (BMI >25).

expanded_sections.heading: Kaskade Iskemik dan Konsep Penumbra

content_blocks.text: ISCHEMIC CASCADE: Within seconds of vessel occlusion, the ischemic cascade begins: (1) ENERGY FAILURE - cessation of oxidative phosphorylation, ATP depletion, ion pump dysfunction (Na+/K+-ATPase, Ca2+-ATPase); (2) MEMBRANE DEPOLARIZATION - influx of Na+, Cl-, H2O (cytotoxic edema), efflux of K+; (3) EXCITOTOXICITY - massive release of glutamate into synaptic cleft, overstimulation of NMDA and AMPA receptors, excessive Ca2+ influx; (4) CALCIUM OVERLOAD - activates lipases, proteases, nucleases, NO synthase, leading to free radical production; (5) FREE RADICAL FORMATION - reactive oxygen species (ROS) damage lipids, proteins, DNA; (6) INFLAMMATION - leukocyte infiltration, microglial activation, cytokine release, BBB disruption (vasogenic edema); (7) CELL DEATH - necrosis in the core, apoptosis in the penumbra. PENUMBRA CONCEPT: The ischemic penumbra is tissue surrounding the irreversibly damaged infarct core that is hemodynamically compromised but still viable. Cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the penumbra is approximately 10-20 mL/100g/min (normal 50-60). Penumbra tissue can be salvaged with prompt reperfusion. The goal of acute stroke therapy is to save the penumbra. Penumbra exists for a limited time window - typically 3-6 hours, extendable to 24 hours in selected cases with advanced imaging.

bullets: 1. Gagal energi: deplesi ATP
2. Depolarisasi membran: edema sitotoksik
3. Eksitotoksisitas: pelepasan glutamat berlebihan
4. Overload kalsium: aktivasi enzim degradatif
5. Formasi radikal bebas: ROS
6. Inflamasi: infiltrasi leukosit
7. Kematian sel: nekrosis (inti), apoptosis (penumbra)

callouts.text: Penumbra = salvageable tissue around infarct core; the therapeutic target in acute stroke; time-sensitive

content_blocks.text: NEUROPROTECTION: Strategies to protect the ischemic penumbra. Despite many candidates in research, no neuroprotective agent has proven effective in clinical trials. Hypothermia shows promise. Maintaining physiological parameters (normoglycemia, normothermia, normotension) is essential. ACUTE MANAGEMENT: TIME IS BRAIN. IV thrombolysis with alteplase (tPA) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (inclusion: age >=18, measurable deficit, CT excludes hemorrhage; exclusion: recent surgery, active bleeding, INR>1.7, platelets<100k, prior ICH, severe stroke NIHSS>25). Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion (ICA, proximal MCA) up to 24 hours in selected patients (DAWN, DEFUSE 3 trials). Blood pressure management: permissive hypertension in ischemic stroke (up to 220/120) unless thrombolysis candidate (lower to <185/110). Supportive care: airway, oxygenation, hydration, temperature control, glycemic control.

callouts.text: 'Time is brain' - every minute of large vessel occlusion costs 1.9 million neurons

expanded_sections.heading: Aspek Gizi dalam Stroke

content_blocks.text: NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT: Dysphagia screening is mandatory before any oral intake. If unsafe swallow: NGT feeding within 24-48 hours. Target 25-30 kcal/kg/day and 1-1.5 g protein/kg/day. Monitor for aspiration. PREVENTION: DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) - rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, lean protein; low in sodium, saturated fat, added sugars. Mediterranean diet also shows protective effect. Key nutrients: potassium, magnesium, omega-3 fatty acids, folate. Weight management: BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2. Limit sodium to <2.3 g/day (ideally <1.5 g/day for hypertensives).

expanded_sections.heading: Pendahuluan Pemeriksaan Neurologis

content_blocks.text: The neurological examination follows a systematic approach to localize lesions within the nervous system. Components include: mental status, cranial nerves, motor system (inspection, tone, power, bulk), sensory system (modalities, dermatomes), coordination, gait and stance, and reflexes (deep tendon, superficial, pathological). The examination should always be interpreted in the context of the history.

bullets: Status mental
Saraf kranialis
Sistem motorik
Sistem sensorik
Koordinasi
Gait dan sikap
Refleks

content_blocks.text: CN I (Olfactory): smell test with coffee, vanilla, alcohol. CN II (Optic): visual acuity (Snellen chart), visual fields (confrontation), fundoscopy (disc, vessels, macula). CN III, IV, VI (Oculomotor, Trochlear, Abducens): pupil size/shape/reaction (RAPD), extraocular movements (H pattern), nystagmus. CN V (Trigeminal): facial sensation (V1, V2, V3), corneal reflex, masseter/temporalis power, jaw jerk. CN VII (Facial): facial symmetry at rest and with movement (forehead wrinkling, eye closure, smile), taste anterior 2/3 tongue. CN VIII (Vestibulocochlear): hearing (Rinne, Weber), balance. CN IX, X (Glossopharyngeal, Vagus): gag reflex, palatal elevation, voice quality, swallowing. CN XI (Accessory): SCM and trapezius strength. CN XII (Hypoglossal): tongue symmetry, fasciculations, deviation on protrusion.

callouts.text: UMN facial lesion: forehead spared (bilateral innervation); LMN facial lesion: entire face affected including forehead

content_blocks.text: INSPECTION: posture, involuntary movements (tremor, chorea, dystonia, fasciculations), muscle wasting, deformities. TONE: assess resistance to passive movement throughout ROM; hypertonia (spasticity, rigidity) vs hypotonia vs paratonia. STRENGTH: MRC grading 0-5 (0=no contraction, 1=flicker, 2=active movement with gravity eliminated, 3=active movement against gravity, 4=active movement against resistance, 5=normal power). BULK: measure limb circumference, compare sides. UMN vs LMN SIGNS: UMN - spasticity, increased reflexes, Babinski positive, no fasciculations, no atrophy; LMN - flaccidity, decreased/absent reflexes, fasciculations, atrophy.

expanded_sections.heading: Sensorik, Koordinasi, dan Refleks

content_blocks.text: SENSORY EXAMINATION: Test primary modalities - light touch, pinprick (pain), temperature, vibration (128 Hz tuning fork), joint position sense. Compare symmetrical points. Map deficits to dermatomes or peripheral nerve territories. COORDINATION: Finger-to-nose test (upper limb), heel-to-shin test (lower limb), rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia), fine finger movements. Romberg test (proprioception/vestibular function). REFLEXES: Deep tendon reflexes (biceps C5-6, triceps C6-7, supinator C5-6, knee L3-4, ankle S1-2) graded 0-4+. Pathological reflexes: Babinski (UPST, dorsiflexion great toe), Hoffmann, clonus. Primitive reflexes: glabellar, snout, palmomental, grasp. MENINGEAL SIGNS: neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign.

bullets: Sensorik: sentuhan halus, nyeri, suhu, vibrasi, propriosepsi
Koordinasi: finger-nose, heel-shin, dysdiadochokinesia
Refleks: DTR, Babinski, klonus
Tanda meningeal: kaku kuduk, Kernig, Brudzinski

callouts.text: Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) is the most reliable indicator of UMN pathology

expanded_sections.heading: Gait dan Dokumentasi

content_blocks.text: GAIT EXAMINATION: Observe patient walking (heel walking, toe walking, tandem gait). Assess initiation, stride length, arm swing, turning, stability. DOCUMENTATION: Record all findings systematically using standardized formats. Common scales: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) for consciousness, NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) for stroke severity, Modified Rankin Scale (mRS) for disability.

bullets: Gait: inisiasi, panjang langkah, ayunan lengan, stabilitas
GCS: Eye (1-4), Verbal (1-5), Motor (1-5)

expanded_sections.heading: Klasifikasi Pusing

content_blocks.text: Dizziness is classified into four symptom categories to guide the diagnostic approach. VERTIGO: Illusion of movement (spinning, tilting, swaying); indicates vestibular system dysfunction. PRESYNCOPE: Lightheadedness, feeling faint; suggests cardiovascular or systemic cause (orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, anemia). DISEQUILIBRIUM: Unsteadiness, imbalance; suggests proprioceptive, visual, cerebellar, or motor deficits. NONSPECIFIC DIZZINESS: Vague head sensation; may indicate psychiatric (anxiety, hyperventilation), metabolic, or medication causes.

bullets: Vertigo: ilusi gerakan (putar, miring, goyang)
Presinkop: pusing gelap, mau pingsan
Disekuilibrium: tidak stabil, kehilangan keseimbangan
Non-spesifik: sensasi kepala tidak jelas

content_blocks.text: Differentiating peripheral from central vertigo is critical for patient safety. PERIPHERAL VERTIGO: More intense spinning, severe nausea/vomiting, horizontal-rotatory nystagmus with fast phase away from affected ear, fatigable nystagmus, symptoms provoked/worsened by position changes, no neurological deficits, hearing loss may be present (Meniere), direction-fixed nystagmus. CENTRAL VERTIGO: Less intense spinning, mild nausea, vertical/pure vertical nystagmus, non-fatigable, may occur in any position, neurological deficits common (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, weakness, ataxia), no hearing loss, direction-changing nystagmus, severe gait instability.

callouts.text: Vertical nystagmus = central cause until proven otherwise - requires urgent MRI

content_blocks.text: BPPV (BENIGN PAROXYSMAL POSITIONAL VERTIGO): Brief episodes (<1 minute) of intense spinning triggered by specific head positions; caused by otoconia displacement in posterior semicircular canal; diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike maneuver; treated with Epley canalith repositioning maneuver. MENIERE DISEASE: Episodes lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness; endolymphatic hydrops; dietary salt restriction, diuretics. VESTIBULAR NEURITIS: Sudden onset severe vertigo lasting days, post-viral, no hearing loss; positive head impulse test toward affected side; treated with steroids, antiemetics, vestibular rehabilitation. VESTIBULAR MIGRAINE: Vertigo episodes 5 minutes to 72 hours, migraine history, photophobia/phonophobia during vertigo; treated with migraine prophylaxis.

expanded_sections.heading: HINTS Examination

content_blocks.text: HINTS examination is a three-component bedside test for acute vestibular syndrome (AVS: acute onset continuous vertigo with nystagmus, nausea, imbalance lasting >24 hours). It is MORE SENSITIVE than MRI for detecting stroke in the first 24-48 hours. H - HEAD IMPULSE TEST: Rapid head turn while patient fixates on examiner's nose. Normal (corrective saccade) = peripheral lesion = reassuring. Abnormal (no corrective saccade) = central lesion = dangerous. I - NYSTAGMUS: Direction-changing nystagmus on gaze = central. Direction-fixed = more likely peripheral. Vertical nystagmus = central. N - TEST OF SKEW: Alternate cover test looking for vertical correction movement. Skew deviation present = central lesion. INTERPRETATION: Any one abnormal component = central cause = urgent MRI. All three normal = peripheral cause. HINTS PLUS: Add hearing test (fingers rub); acute hearing loss with AVS suggests AICA stroke (central).

bullets: H: Head impulse - normal (saccade korektif) = perifer; abnormal = sentral
I: Nistagmus - direction-changing = sentral; vertikal = sentral
N: Test of skew - skew deviation = sentral
Salah satu abnormal = sentral (stroke), MRI segera
HINTS PLUS: tambah tes pendengaran (AICA stroke)

callouts.text: HINTS is MORE sensitive than MRI for stroke in the first 24-48 hours of AVS

expanded_sections.heading: Algoritma Diagnostik

content_blocks.text: DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH: Step 1 - Classify symptom type (vertigo vs presyncope vs disequilibrium vs nonspecific). Step 2 - If vertigo: determine timing (seconds/minutes/hours/days/continuous). Step 3 - Apply HINTS if AVS present. Step 4 - Perform Dix-Hallpike if brief positional vertigo. Step 5 - Look for red flags: new headache, neurological deficits, severe gait instability, vertical nystagmus, direction-changing nystagmus, vascular risk factors. RED FLAGS requiring urgent imaging: any central signs on HINTS, associated neurological deficits, severe continuous vertigo in high-risk vascular patient, head trauma, new severe headache.

key_points: Balance depends on integration of vestibular (inner ear), visual, and proprioceptive (somatosensory) systems processed by the cerebellum and brainstem
Romberg test evaluates proprioception; sharpened Romberg adds challenge

expanded_sections.heading: Anatomi Sistem Keseimbangan

content_blocks.text: Balance is maintained by integration of three sensory systems: VESTIBULAR SYSTEM (inner ear - semicircular canals for angular acceleration, otolith organs for linear acceleration/gravity); VISUAL SYSTEM (provides spatial orientation and reference); and PROPRIoCEPTIVE/SOMATOSENSORY SYSTEM (joint position sense, muscle spindle input from feet and legs). These inputs are integrated in the CEREBELLUM and BRAINSTEM vestibular nuclei, with output to oculomotor system (VOR) and postural muscles. Dysfunction in any system or the integrator can cause imbalance.

bullets: Sistem vestibular: kanal semisirkular, organ otolit
Sistem visual: orientasi spasial
Sistem proprioseptif: posisi sendi, sensor kaki
Integrasi: serebelum, nukleus vestibular batang otak

expanded_sections.heading: Pendekatan Klinis

content_blocks.text: HISTORY: Characterize the dizziness (spinning vs lightheaded vs imbalance), duration (seconds/minutes/hours/days), triggers (position change, head movement, standing), associated symptoms (hearing loss, tinnitus, nausea, neurological symptoms), and medical history (hypertension, diabetes, medications). KEY QUESTIONS: Is it true vertigo or non-vertiginous dizziness? Is it constant or episodic? What triggers it? Are there auditory symptoms? Are there neurological symptoms?

Durasi: detik/menit/jam/hari
Pemicu: perubahan posisi, gerakan kepala, berdiri
Gejala penyerta: gangguan dengar, tinitus, mual, defisit neurologis

content_blocks.text: ROMBERG TEST: Stand feet together, eyes closed; positive if sway/fall increases with eyes closed (indicates proprioceptive or vestibular loss). SHARPENED ROMBERG: Tandem stance (heel-to-toe), eyes closed. FUKUDA STEPPING TEST: March in place with eyes closed for 50 steps; rotation >30 degrees or forward/backward displacement >50cm suggests unilateral vestibular hypofunction. UNTERBERGER TEST: March in place with eyes closed and arms raised; rotation toward affected side indicates unilateral vestibular lesion. HEAD IMPULSE TEST: Rapid head turn while fixating; catch-up saccade indicates reduced VOR on that side. DIX-HALLPIKE: For BPPV diagnosis - head hanging precipitates rotatory nystagmus. GAIT EXAMINATION: Observe initiation, stride, arm swing, turning, tandem walking.
