expanded_sections.heading: Pemeriksaan Penunjang

content_blocks.text: AUDIOGRAM: Pure tone audiometry, speech audiometry, tympanometry. Sensorineural hearing loss with low-frequency component suggests Meniere; asymmetric hearing loss suggests acoustic neuroma. VNG (VIDEO NYSTAGMOGRAPHY): Records eye movements to assess vestibular function. Includes spontaneous nystagmus, gaze testing, smooth pursuit, saccades, optokinetic nystagmus, positional testing, and caloric testing. CALORIC TEST: Gold standard for assessing individual horizontal semicircular canal function. Warm (44C) and cool (30C) water irrigation. Normal response: nystagmus toward irrigated ear with warm, away with cool. Canal paresis: reduced response on one side. Directional preponderance: stronger response in one direction. POSTUROGRAPHY: Computerized platform measuring postural sway under various conditions (eyes open/closed, platform stable/moving).

bullets: Audiogram: SNHL low-freq = Meniere; asimetris = neuroma akustik
VNG: nistagmus spontan, smooth pursuit, saccade, kalorik
Tes kalorik: standar emas fungsi kanal horizontal
Posturografi: ukur sway postural

content_blocks.text: BPPV: Epley maneuver for posterior canal; Brandt-Daroff exercises; rare cases require surgery. MENIERE: Low-salt diet, diuretics, betahistine; intratympanic gentamicin or steroids for refractory; endolymphatic sac surgery. VESTIBULAR NEURITIS: Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) within 72 hours, antiemetics, early vestibular rehabilitation. ACOUSTIC NEUROMA (Vestibular Schwannoma): MRI with contrast; management options include observation, stereotactic radiosurgery, or microsurgical removal depending on size and symptoms. BILATERAL VESTIBULOPATHY: From ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides), meningitis, autoimmune disorders; vestibular rehabilitation is mainstay. PPPD (Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness): Chronic non-spinning dizziness >3 months, worse with upright posture and complex visual stimuli; treated with SSRIs (sertraline), CBT, and desensitization exercises.

modules.overview: Kuliah radiologi tentang tumor otak yang mencakup karakteristik pencitraan glioma (grade rendah dan tinggi), meningioma, adenoma hipofisis, schwannoma (neuroma akustik), metastasis, dan limfoma. Membahas temuan CT dan MRI termasuk pola penyangatan kontras, karakteristik difusi, fitur spektroskopi, dan diagnosis banding berdasarkan fitur pencitraan. Menerapkan fitur pencitraan untuk membedakan metastasis dari tumor primer
key_points: High-grade gliomas show irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, surrounding edema, mass effect
Meningioma: extra-axial, broad dural base, homogeneous enhancement, dural tail sign
Acoustic neuroma: CPA mass, extends into internal auditory canal (ice cream cone sign)
Pituitary adenoma: sellar mass, may extend suprasellar (snowman sign), cavernous sinus invasion
Metastases: typically multiple, at gray-white junction, disproportionate edema to size

content_blocks.text: GLIOMAS are primary brain tumors arising from glial cells. LOW-GRADE GLIOMA (WHO Grade II): CT shows hypodense or isodense lesion, may have calcification, minimal or no enhancement. MRI T1 shows hypointense, T2/FLAIR shows hyperintense, typically well-defined, minimal surrounding edema, no necrosis. Slow-growing, may transform to high-grade. HIGH-GRADE GLIOMA (WHO Grade III-IV, glioblastoma): CT shows irregular hypodense center (necrosis) with ring-enhancing margins, significant surrounding hypodensity (vasogenic edema), mass effect. MRI T1 shows heterogeneous with ring enhancement, T2/FLAIR shows extensive hyperintense edema beyond tumor margin, central necrosis appears hyperintense on DWI (restricted diffusion in tumor). Glioblastoma shows thick irregular ring enhancement with central necrosis, often crosses corpus callosum (butterfly glioma). Spectroscopy shows elevated choline, reduced NAA, lactate/lipid peak.

callouts.text: Glioblastoma crossing corpus callosum = 'butterfly' appearance; highly characteristic

expanded_sections.heading: Meningioma dan Adenoma Hipofisis

content_blocks.text: MENINGIOMA: Extra-axial tumor from meningothelial cells. CT shows hyperdense (isodense to brain), may have calcification (psammomatous), intense homogeneous enhancement, hyperostosis of adjacent bone. MRI T1 isointense to cortex, intense homogeneous enhancement, dural tail sign (tumor extension along dura), CSF cleft sign (cleavage plane between tumor and brain). PITUITARY ADENOMA: Sellar mass. Microadenoma (<10mm): hypointense on T1 compared to normal pituitary, enhances less than surrounding gland on dynamic contrast (appears as non-enhancing focus). Macroadenoma (>=10mm): expands sella, may extend suprasellar (compressing optic chiasm - bitemporal hemianopia), cavernous sinus invasion (encasing ICA), inferior extension into sphenoid sinus. Snowman sign when suprasellar extension is constricted by diaphragma sellae.

bullets: Meningioma: ekstra-aksial, dural tail sign, hiperostosis
Adenoma hipofisis: mikro <10mm, makro >=10mm
Makroadenoma: ekstensi suprasellar (snowman sign), invasi sinus kavernosus

callouts.text: Dural tail sign = dural enhancement extending from tumor margin; classic for meningioma but not pathognomonic

content_blocks.text: SCHWANNOMA (ACOUSTIC NEUROMA/VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA): CPA (cerebellopontine angle) mass originating from vestibular nerve. CT shows widening of internal auditory canal (IAC). MRI T1 shows hypointense to isointense, intense enhancement, extends into IAC creating 'ice cream cone' appearance. Larger tumors may compress brainstem and cerebellum, cause hydrocephalus. Cystic components common in larger tumors. METASTASES: Most common brain tumors in adults. Typically multiple lesions at gray-white matter junction. CT shows hypodense (may be hyperdense if hemorrhagic). MRI T1 hypointense with ring or homogeneous enhancement, T2/FLAIR shows disproportionate surrounding edema compared to size of enhancing lesion. Common primary sources: lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colon. Hemorrhagic metastases: melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, thyroid, lung.

callouts.text: CPA mass extending into IAC = vestibular schwannoma until proven otherwise

expanded_sections.heading: Limfoma dan Diagnosis Banding

content_blocks.text: PRIMARY CNS LYMPHOMA: Typically B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Immunocompetent: solitary or few periventricular lesions, homogeneous enhancement (disrupted BBB), hyperdense on CT (high cellularity), restricted diffusion on DWI (high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio), extends along ependymal or meningeal surfaces. Immunocompromised (HIV): ring-enhancing lesions, may be indistinguishable from toxoplasmosis; EBV PCR in CSF is diagnostic. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS APPROACH: Location (intra-axial vs extra-axial), single vs multiple, age, enhancement pattern, associated findings (edema, calcification, hemorrhage, bone changes). Key differentiators: Glioblastoma (ring-enhancing, necrosis, crosses corpus callosum); Abscess (thin smooth ring, restricted diffusion in center); Metastasis (multiple, gray-white junction, known primary); Lymphoma (periventricular, homogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion).

Limfoma immunokompromai: ring-enhancing, sulit dibedakan dari toksoplasmosis
Diagnosis banding: lokasi, jumlah, pola enhancement

callouts.text: Primary CNS lymphoma: periventricular, homogeneous enhancement, marked restricted diffusion (high cellularity)

modules.title: Status Epileptikus
modules.overview: Kuliah komprehensif tentang status epileptikus (SE) yang mencakup definisi (definisi 5-menit dan 30-menit), klasifikasi (konvulsif vs non-konvulsif, generalisasi vs fokal), epidemiologi, etiologi, patofisiologi (eksitotoksisitas, disfungsi autonomik), gambaran klinis, pendekatan diagnosis (laboratorium, EEG, neuroimaging), protokol manajemen bertahap (benzodiazepin, fenytoin/valproat, SE refrakter dengan agen anestesi), komplikasi, dan prognosis. Menekankan algoritma terapi yang bergantung pada waktu di mana keterlambatan memperburuk outcome.
learning_goals: Mendefinisikan status epileptikus menggunakan kriteria berbasis waktu
Mengklasifikasikan SE ke dalam tipe konvulsif dan non-konvulsif
Menerapkan protokol terapi bertahap untuk SE
Menatalaksana status epileptikus refrakter dengan agen anestesi
key_points: Operational definition: 5 minutes of continuous seizures OR two or more discrete seizures without full recovery between
Time-dependent treatment: benzodiazepines (0-5 min), IV antiepileptics (5-20 min), anesthetic agents (20-60 min) for refractory SE
Mortality increases with duration: ~3% at 10-29 min, 19% at >30 min, 32% at >60 min
Non-convulsive SE (NCSE) requires EEG for diagnosis - maintain high index of suspicion in altered mental status after seizure
Refractory SE requires continuous EEG monitoring, anesthetic agents (midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital), and ICU-level care

content_blocks.text: STATUS EPILEPTICUS (SE) is defined as: (1) 5 minutes or more of continuous clinical and/or electrographic seizure activity; OR (2) recurrent seizure activity without recovery (return to baseline) between seizures. Operational time points: T1 (5 minutes) = time when treatment should begin; T2 (30 minutes) = time when risk of neuronal injury increases significantly. CLASSIFICATION: By motor activity: Convulsive SE (CSE) = tonic-clonic movements; Non-convulsive SE (NCSE) = altered mental status without convulsions; Myoclonic SE. By EEG pattern: Generalized SE; Focal SE. By treatment response: Early SE (0-5 min); Established SE (5-20 min, responds to first-line); Refractory SE (RSE) (20-60 min, fails first and second line); Super-refractory SE (>60 min or recurs after anesthetic withdrawal).

callouts.text: Do not wait 30 minutes to treat - begin treatment at 5 minutes per operational definition

expanded_sections.heading: Etiologi dan Patofisiologi

content_blocks.text: ETIOLOGY: Acute symptomatic (stroke, trauma, infection, metabolic derangement, hypoxia, drug withdrawal); Remote symptomatic (epilepsy with breakthrough seizures, missed medications); Progressive symptomatic (brain tumor, neurodegenerative disease). Common triggers: antiepileptic drug non-adherence (most common in known epileptics), alcohol withdrawal, CNS infection, stroke, metabolic (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, uremia, hepatic encephalopathy). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Initially, compensatory mechanisms maintain seizure threshold (increased GABA, enhanced receptor sensitivity). After 30 minutes, these fail: GABA receptors internalize (reduced sensitivity to benzodiazepines), NMDA receptors traffic to surface (enhanced excitotoxicity), autonomic dysfunction (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, sweating, arrhythmias), excitotoxic neuronal damage (glutamate surge, calcium influx, free radical production).

bullets: Penyebab: stroke, trauma, infeksi, metabolic, hipoksia, withdraw obat
Pemicu paling umum: non-adherensi OAE, withdraw alkohol
Setelah 30 menit: internalisasi reseptor GABA, eksitotoksisitas
Disfungsi autonomik: hipertensi, takikardi, hipertermi

callouts.text: After 30 minutes, GABA receptor internalization makes benzodiazepines less effective - this is why early treatment is critical

expanded_sections.heading: Gambaran Klinis dan Diagnosis

content_blocks.text: CONVULSIVE SE: Generalized tonic-clonic activity lasting >5 minutes; may become subtle (decreased motor activity) after 30-60 min despite ongoing EEG seizure activity; coma between seizures without recovery; autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, pupillary changes); respiratory compromise. NON-CONVULSIVE SE: Altered mental status (confusion, decreased responsiveness, coma) without convulsive activity; may follow CSE (patient fails to wake up after clinical seizures stop); requires EEG for diagnosis. EEG patterns: spike-wave at 3 Hz (typical absence), focal rhythmic activity, periodic discharges. DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP: Blood glucose (immediately), electrolytes (Na, Ca, Mg), renal function, LFTs, ABG, toxicology screen, antiepileptic drug levels, CBC. CT head to rule out structural cause. LP if infection suspected. EEG as soon as possible (especially if NCSE suspected or RSE management).

bullets: CSE: aktivitas tonik-klonik >5 menit, disfungsi autonomik
NCSE: altered mental status tanpa konvulsi, butuh EEG
Pemeriksaan: gula darah, elektrolit, CT kepala, EEG
LP jika dicurigai infeksi

callouts.text: Always check blood glucose first in any seizure presentation - hypoglycemia is reversible and treatable

content_blocks.text: PHASE 1 - STABILIZATION (0-5 min): ABCs, vital signs, IV access, blood glucose, labs, position patient to prevent injury, O2 if needed. PHASE 2 - FIRST-LINE (0-10 min): Benzodiazepines (most effective in first 20 min). Options: Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg), may repeat once; OR Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM (if no IV access) or 0.2 mg/kg buccal/IN; OR Diazepam 0.15-0.2 mg/kg IV. PHASE 3 - SECOND-LINE (10-20 min): If seizures continue after benzodiazepines. ONE of: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV at max 50 mg/min (monitor BP, ECG); OR Valproate 30-40 mg/kg IV; OR Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (up to 4500 mg); OR Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV. PHASE 4 - REFRACTORY SE (20-60 min): If seizures continue after adequate first and second line. Admit to ICU, intubate if needed, continuous EEG. ONE of: Midazolam infusion 0.2 mg/kg bolus then 0.05-2 mg/kg/h; OR Propofol 1-2 mg/kg bolus then 20-100 mcg/kg/min (caution: propofol infusion syndrome >48h); OR Pentobarbital 5-15 mg/kg bolus then 0.5-5 mg/kg/h.

callouts.text: Doses are maximums - always monitor vitals during phenytoin infusion (hypotension, arrhythmia risk)

expanded_sections.heading: SE Refrakter dan Prognosis

content_blocks.text: REFRACTORY SE MANAGEMENT: ICU admission, continuous EEG monitoring (burst suppression or seizure suppression for 24-48h before weaning), supportive care (mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic support, temperature management). Treat underlying cause. Consider alternative diagnoses (pseudoseizures, metabolic coma). COMPLICATIONS: Cardiovascular (arrhythmia, hypotension, cardiac arrest), respiratory (aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure), neurological (excitotoxic injury, cerebral edema, permanent cognitive deficits), metabolic (rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, DIC), autonomic storm. PROGNOSIS: Mortality 10-20% for GCSE overall. Factors associated with worse outcome: older age, longer SE duration, acute symptomatic etiology, refractory SE, comorbidities. Good prognostic factors: younger age, idiopathic/cryptogenic etiology, shorter duration, prompt treatment. Mortality by duration: ~3% at 10-29 min, 19% at >30 min, 32% at >60 min.

bullets: RSE: ICU, EEG kontinu, ventilasi mekanik jika diperlukan
Komplikasi: aritmia, aspirasi, cedera otak, rabdomiolisis
Mortalitas: 10-20% GCSE; meningkat dengan durasi
Faktor buruk: usia tua, durasi panjang, refrakter

callouts.text: Mortality increases with every minute of untreated SE - aggressive early treatment is the key to improving outcomes

modules.title: Stroke Radiology
modules.overview: Kuliah radiologi tentang pencitraan stroke yang mencakup temuan CT pada stroke iskemik akut (tanda awal, skor ASPECTS), karakteristik CT stroke hemoragik, sekuens MRI untuk evaluasi stroke (DWI, FLAIR, GRE/SWI, MRA), pencitraan vaskular (CTA, MRA, DSA), dan tindak lanjut pencitraan pasca-terapi. Menekankan tanda CT awal yang mengindikasikan oklusi vaskular besar dan peran pencitraan lanjut dalam memperpanjang jendela terapi.

Menerapkan skoring ASPECTS untuk stroke sirkulasi anterior
Membedakan stroke iskemik dan hemoragik pada CT
Menginterpretasi DWI dan MRA untuk evaluasi stroke
key_points: Non-contrast CT is first-line to exclude hemorrhage in acute stroke
ASPECTS score (0-10) quantifies early ischemic changes; score <7 suggests large infarct with poor thrombolysis outcome
Hyperdense MCA sign indicates thrombus in the vessel - key sign for thrombectomy candidacy
DWI shows restricted diffusion within minutes of ischemia onset; FLAIR may be normal in first 3-6 hours
DWI-FLAIR mismatch can identify patients within 4.5-hour window for thrombolysis

evidence_map.note: CT in acute stroke: early signs and ASPECTS

expanded_sections.heading: Pendekatan Pencitraan Stroke

content_blocks.text: The imaging workup for acute stroke follows a structured protocol. Step 1: Non-contrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage (first-line, immediate). Step 2: If no hemorrhage and within treatment window, assess for early ischemic changes and large vessel occlusion signs. Step 3: CT angiography (CTA) from aortic arch to vertex to identify large vessel occlusion. Step 4: CT perfusion (CTP) or MRI (DWI, FLAIR, MRA) for advanced assessment in extended window candidates. Step 5: Post-treatment imaging to assess for hemorrhagic transformation and reperfusion.

bullets: CT non-kontras: pertama untuk eksklusi perdarahan
CTA: deteksi okulsi vaskular besar
CTP/MRI: untuk jendela waktu yang diperpanjang
Pasca-terapi: evaluasi transformasi hemoragik

expanded_sections.heading: CT pada Stroke Akut
expanded_sections.subheading: CT in Acute Stroke - Early Signs and ASPECTS

content_blocks.text: EARLY CT SIGNS OF ISCHEMIA (<6 hours): Loss of insular ribbon, loss of lentiform nucleus definition (basal ganglia obscuration), hemispheric sulcal effacement, hyperdense MCA sign (thrombus density within vessel), hypodensity in MCA territory. These signs indicate established ischemia and potential large vessel occlusion. ASPECTS SCORE (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score): 10-point scoring system assessing MCA territory regions. Regions: caudate (C), lentiform nucleus (L), internal capsule (IC), insular ribbon (I), anterior MCA cortex (M1), MCA cortex lateral to insula (M2), posterior MCA cortex (M3), anterior MCA cortex superior (M4), lateral MCA cortex superior (M5), posterior MCA cortex superior (M6). Normal = 10 points; each region with early ischemic change loses 1 point. Score 7-10: favorable for thrombolysis. Score 0-6: large infarct, higher hemorrhage risk with thrombolysis.

callouts.text: ASPECTS <7 suggests large core infarct; higher risk of hemorrhagic transformation with thrombolysis

content_blocks.text: DWI (DIFFUSION-WEIGHTED IMAGING): Most sensitive sequence for acute ischemia; shows restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, dark on ADC) within minutes of onset; remains abnormal for 7-10 days (pseudonormalization occurs around day 10-14). FLAIR: Hyperintensity indicates vasogenic edema; may be normal in first 3-6 hours (DWI-FLAIR mismatch). T2*: GRE/SWI shows hemorrhage as hypointense (blooming artifact); sensitive for microbleeds and hemorrhagic transformation. MRA: Non-invasive vascular imaging; shows vessel occlusion, stenosis, aneurysm. DWI-FLAIR MISMATCH: DWI positive but FLAIR negative indicates stroke onset <4.5-6 hours; used to select patients for thrombolysis when onset time is unknown (WAKE-UP trial).

callouts.text: DWI-FLAIR mismatch = onset <4.5-6 hours; can guide thrombolysis in unknown onset stroke

expanded_sections.heading: Pencitraan Vaskular

content_blocks.text: CTA (CT ANGIOGRAPHY): Fast, widely available; requires iodinated contrast; shows vessel occlusion, stenosis, dissection; source images and MIP reconstructions. MRA (MR ANGIOGRAPHY): Non-contrast (time-of-flight) or contrast-enhanced; no radiation; longer acquisition time; sensitive for intracranial and extracranial vessel assessment. DSA (DIGITAL SUBTRACTION ANGIOGRAPHY): Gold standard for vascular imaging; invasive; used for pre-thrombectomy assessment and for diagnosis when CTA/MRA is inconclusive; catheter-based with direct contrast injection. Carotid Doppler ultrasound: Non-invasive screening for carotid stenosis; assesses plaque morphology and hemodynamic significance.

bullets: CTA: cepat, kontras yodium, okulsi/stenosis
MRA: tanpa radiasi, ToF atau kontras
DSA: standar emas, invasif, pra-trombektomi
Doppler karotis: skrining stenosis non-invasif

expanded_sections.heading: Stroke Hemoragik dan Pasca-Terapi

content_blocks.text: HEMORRHAGIC STROKE ON CT: Acute blood appears hyperdense (60-80 HU) due to hemoglobin; density decreases over time (7-10 days becomes isodense, >2-3 weeks hypodense). Location suggests etiology: basal ganglia/thalamus (hypertension), lobar (amyloid angiopathy in elderly, AVM in young), cerebellar/pontine (hypertension). IVH (intraventricular hemorrhage) suggests extension from parenchymal bleed. SAH: blood in sulci, cisterns, ventricles; aneurysm is most common cause. HEMORRHAGIC TRANSFORMATION (HT): Conversion of ischemic infarct to hemorrhage; classified as HI-1 (petechiae around infarct), HI-2 (confluent petechiae without mass effect), PH-1 (hematoma <30% of infarct with mild mass effect), PH-2 (hematoma >30% or significant mass effect). Risk factors: large infarct, reperfusion therapy, uncontrolled hypertension, anticoagulation. PH-2 associated with worse outcome.

bullets: Darah akut: hiperdens 60-80 HU
Basal ganglia/talamus: hipertensi; Lobar: amiloid/AVM
HT: HI-1/2 (petekie), PH-1/2 (hematoma)
PH-2: outcome lebih buruk

callouts.text: Hyperdense MCA sign + ASPECTS >=7 = good thrombectomy candidate

modules.overview: Kuliah komprehensif tentang trauma sistem saraf yang mencakup klasifikasi trauma kepala (tertutup vs penetrasi, cedera primer vs sekunder), beratnya TBI (ringan, sedang, berat menggunakan GCS), konkusio, kontusio serebri, diffuse axonal injury (DAI), hematoma epidural, hematoma subdural, perdarahan subaraknoid traumatis, fraktur tengkorak, cedera saraf tulang belakang (lengkap vs tidak lengkap), dan kegawatan neurobedah. Menyertakan temuan pencitraan pada CT dan MRI, prinsip manajemen mengikuti panduan ATLS dan Brain Trauma Foundation.
learning_goals: Mengklasifikasikan beratnya TBI menggunakan GCS
Membedakan hematoma epidural dari subdural pada CT
Mengenali diffuse axonal injury pada MRI

key_points: GCS classifies TBI: mild (13-15), moderate (9-12), severe (3-8)
Epidural hematoma: lens-shaped (biconvex), arterial (middle meningeal artery), does not cross sutures
Subdural hematoma: crescent-shaped, venous (bridging veins), crosses suture lines but not dural attachments
DAI: small punctate hemorrhages at gray-white junction, corpus callosum, brainstem; best seen on GRE/SWI MRI
Secondary brain injury (hypotension, hypoxia, hyperthermia) is preventable and must be aggressively managed

evidence_map.note: TBI severity, GCS, primary vs secondary injury
Specific traumatic lesions: EDH, SDH, contusion, DAI

content_blocks.text: Head trauma is classified by mechanism: CLOSED (non-penetrating, most common) vs OPEN/PENETRATING (skull fracture with dural breach). By injury timing: PRIMARY (direct mechanical damage at moment of impact - contusion, hematoma, laceration, DAI) vs SECONDARY (subsequent physiological insults - hypoxia, hypotension, edema, increased ICP, excitotoxicity). Secondary injury is preventable and is the main target of neurocritical care. TBI SEVERITY by GCS: MILD (GCS 13-15, brief loss of consciousness <30 min, no structural lesion on CT); MODERATE (GCS 9-12, LOC 30 min - 24h, abnormal CT findings); SEVERE (GCS 3-8, LOC >24h, significant CT abnormalities).

callouts.text: Preventing secondary brain injury (hypotension, hypoxia) is the key to improving TBI outcomes

expanded_sections.heading: Cedera Primer vs Sekunder

content_blocks.text: PRIMARY INJURY (irreversible): Direct mechanical damage to brain tissue at moment of impact. Includes: cerebral contusion (bruising of brain surface, coup-contrecoup pattern), diffuse axonal injury (shearing of axons from rotational acceleration/deceleration), hematomas (EDH, SDH, ICH), skull fractures, brain laceration. SECONDARY INJURY (preventable): Cascading physiological and biochemical events following primary injury. Main causes: HYPOTENSION (SBP <90 mmHg is the most important predictor of poor outcome), HYPOXIA (SpO2 <90%, PaO2 <60 mmHg), HYPER/HYPOCAPNIA, HYPERGLYCEMIA, HYPERTHERMIA (fever worsens outcome), increased ICP, excitotoxicity, free radical production, inflammation. Management targets: maintain SBP >90 mmHg (adults) or age-appropriate MAP in children, SpO2 >94%, PaCO2 35-40 mmHg, normoglycemia (80-180 mg/dL), normothermia, ICP <22 mmHg, CPP 60-70 mmHg.

bullets: Primer: kontusio, DAI, hematoma, fraktur (irreversible)
Sekunder: hipotensi, hipoksia, hipertermi (PREVENTABLE)
Target: SBP >90, SpO2 >94%, normotermia, ICP <22

callouts.text: Single episode of SBP <90 mmHg in TBI doubles mortality

content_blocks.text: EPIDURAL HEMATOMA (EDH): Arterial origin (middle meningeal artery in 85%). CT: lens-shaped (biconvex/lenticular), hyperdense, well-defined margins, does NOT cross suture lines. Classic presentation: lucid interval (conscious after injury, then deteriorates). Neurosurgical emergency - evacuation within 1-2 hours of deterioration has excellent outcome. SUBDURAL HEMATOMA (SDH): Venous origin (torn bridging veins). CT: crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines, may be bilateral. Acute (<3 days): hyperdense; Subacute (3-21 days): isodense; Chronic (>21 days): hypodense. Higher mortality than EDH due to associated parenchymal injury. CEREBRAL CONTUSION: Bruising of brain parenchyma, typically frontal and temporal lobes (coup site and contrecoup). CT: patchy hemorrhagic areas, surrounding edema. May expand over 24-48 hours - repeat CT indicated. DIFFUSE AXONAL INJURY (DAI): Shearing injury from rotational acceleration/deceleration. CT often normal or shows small petechial hemorrhages. MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintense foci at gray-white junction, corpus callosum, brainstem; GRE/SWI shows small hemorrhages. Grade 1 (mild): cerebral hemispheres; Grade 2 (moderate): plus corpus callosum; Grade 3 (severe): plus brainstem. Poor prognosis correlates with grade.

callouts.text: EDH = lens-shaped, arterial, lucid interval, does not cross sutures; SDH = crescent-shaped, venous, crosses sutures

expanded_sections.heading: Fraktur Tengkorak dan Cedera Saraf Tulang Belakang
expanded_sections.subheading: Skull Fractures and Spinal Cord Injury

content_blocks.text: SKULL FRACTURES: Linear (most common, usually benign), depressed (surgical elevation if depth >thickness of skull), basilar (battle sign - mastoid ecchymosis, raccoon eyes - periorbital ecchymosis, CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea, hemotympanum), compound/open (surgical emergency), diastatic (suture separation in children). Indications for surgery: depressed fracture >thickness of adjacent skull, open/compound fracture, CSF leak, cosmetic deformity, signs of infection. SPINAL CORD INJURY: Complete (no motor/sensory function below level including sacral segments S4-S5) vs Incomplete (some preserved function below level). Key incomplete syndromes: Central cord syndrome (upper limbs > lower limbs, cervical hyperextension injury); Anterior cord syndrome (motor and pain/temperature loss preserved proprioception/vibration, anterior spinal artery territory); Brown-Sequard syndrome (ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss, hemisection); Posterior cord syndrome (loss of proprioception/vibration, preserved motor/pain/temperature). Spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, areflexia below level for days to weeks after injury; resolves with return of reflexes (may become spastic). Neurogenic shock: hypotension with bradycardia due to loss of sympathetic tone (T6 and above).

callouts.text: Basilar skull fracture signs: Battle sign (mastoid ecchymosis), raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis), CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea

expanded_sections.heading: Manajemen Trauma Kepala
expanded_sections.subheading: TBI Management per ATLS and BTF Guidelines

content_blocks.text: INITIAL MANAGEMENT (ATLS): Primary survey (ABCDE), immobilize C-spine, GCS assessment, pupil examination, FAST exam. INDICATIONS FOR CT HEAD (NICE/SCAN guidelines): GCS <13 at any time, GCS 13-15 with risk factors (LOC, amnesia, vomiting, seizure, focal deficit, coagulopathy, age >65, dangerous mechanism), skull fracture signs, penetrating injury. ICP MANAGEMENT (BTF guidelines): Indications for ICP monitoring: severe TBI (GCS <=8) with abnormal CT, or severe TBI with normal CT plus 2 of: age >40, unilateral/bilateral motor posturing, SBP <90. ICP target <22 mmHg. CPP target 60-70 mmHg (adults). OSMOTHERAPY: Mannitol 0.25-1 g/kg IV (draws water from brain, also improves blood rheology); Hypertonic saline 3% (preferred if hypotensive); serum osmolarity <320 mOsm/L. SURGICAL INDICATIONS: EDH >30 mL regardless of GCS; Acute SDH with thickness >10 mm or midline shift >5 mm; Contusion with volume >50 mL or significant mass effect; Depressed skull fracture >thickness of skull; Open/compound fracture.

modules.title: Tumor Cerebri
modules.overview: Kuliah komprehensif tentang tumor otak yang mencakup klasifikasi (primer vs metastatik, intra-aksial vs ekstra-aksial, grading WHO), presentasi klinis (gejala umum peningkatan ICP, defisit neurologis fokal, kejang), tumor otak primer umum (glioma, meningioma, adenoma hipofisis, schwannoma), tumor otak metastatik, pendekatan diagnosis (neuroimaging dengan MRI sebagai standar emas, biopsi), dan prinsip manajemen (bedah, radioterapi, kemoterapi, manajemen simtomatik termasuk steroid untuk edema dan antiepileptik untuk kontrol kejang).
learning_goals: Mengklasifikasikan tumor otak berdasarkan asal, lokasi, dan grade
Mengenali pola presentasi klinis tumor otak
Menginterpretasi temuan MRI untuk tumor otak yang umum
Menerapkan pendekatan manajemen multidisiplin
key_points: Primary CNS tumors: gliomas (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma) are most common malignant; meningioma most common benign
Metastases are the most common brain tumors overall (lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colon)
General symptoms: headache (worse in morning, with Valsalva), nausea/vomiting, papilledema, cognitive/personality changes
MRI with contrast is gold standard for brain tumor imaging
Dexamethasone 4-10 mg q6h for vasogenic edema; antiepileptics only if seizures have occurred

content_blocks.text: Brain tumors are classified by: ORIGIN (primary CNS tumors vs metastatic); LOCATION (intra-axial within brain parenchyma vs extra-axial outside brain tissue); HISTOLOGY (WHO classification grades I-IV). PRIMARY CNS TUMORS: Gliomas arise from glial cells - astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma, glioblastoma. Meningiomas from arachnoid cap cells. Pituitary adenomas. Schwannomas (vestibular). Primary CNS lymphoma. METASTATIC BRAIN TUMORS: Most common brain tumors in adults; typically multiple; sources: lung (40-50%), breast (15-20%), melanoma (10%), kidney, colon. WHO GRADING: Grade I (benign, slow-growing, curable with surgery); Grade II (low-grade, infiltrative, may recur); Grade III (anaplastic, malignant); Grade IV (highly malignant, rapid growth, necrosis).

expanded_sections.heading: Presentasi Klinis

content_blocks.text: GENERAL SYMPTOMS (increased ICP): Headache (progressive, worse in morning, with coughing/straining/Valsalva), nausea and vomiting (often projectile, worse in morning), papilledema (blurred vision, transient visual obscurations), altered mental status (cognitive slowing, personality changes, somnolence), seizures (may be presenting symptom in 20-40% of brain tumors). FOCAL SYMPTOMS (depend on location): Frontal (personality changes, executive dysfunction, hemiparesis); Temporal (memory deficits, seizures, aphasia); Parietal (sensory loss, neglect, apraxia, Gerstmann syndrome); Occipital (visual field defects); Posterior fossa (ataxia, cranial nerve deficits, hydrocephalus); Brainstem (cranial nerve palsies, long tract signs). PITUITARY/SELLAR: Visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia), endocrine abnormalities.

bullets: Gejala umum: nyeri kepala pagi hari, muntah, papiledema
Kejang: gejala awal pada 20-40% tumor otak
Gejala fokal: tergantung lokalisasi
Pituitary: hemianopia bitemporal, gangguan endokrin

callouts.text: Morning headache that worsens with Valsalva is classic for raised ICP from mass lesion

content_blocks.text: GLIOBLASTOMA MULTIFORME (GBM, WHO Grade IV): Most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults; peak age 45-70; highly infiltrative; MRI shows irregular ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, extensive edema, mass effect, may cross corpus callosum. Treatment: maximal safe resection + concurrent chemoradiation (temozolomide + RT) + adjuvant temozolomide; median survival 15 months. MENINGIOMA (WHO Grade I-III): Most common benign brain tumor; female predominance; extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneous enhancement, dural tail sign; treatment: observation if small/asymptomatic, surgery if symptomatic or growing, radiosurgery for residual/recurrent. PITUITARY ADENOMA: Sellar mass; microadenoma (<10mm) or macroadenoma (>=10mm); visual field defects if suprasellar extension; treatment: medical (prolactinoma - cabergoline/bromocriptine), transsphenoidal surgery, radiation. SCHWANNOMA (VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA, ACOUSTIC NEUROMA): CPA mass from vestibular nerve; unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance; MRI shows enhancing CPA mass extending into IAC; treatment: observation if small, surgery or radiosurgery if growing/symptomatic. PRIMARY CNS LYMPHOMA: Periventricular, homogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion; treatment: high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy.

Metastatic brain tumors are the most common brain tumors in adults. Typically multiple lesions at gray-white matter junction. Common primary sources: lung (40-50%), breast (15-20%), melanoma (10%), renal cell carcinoma, colorectal. MRI: multiple lesions with ring or homogeneous enhancement, disproportionate surrounding edema compared to tumor size. Hemorrhagic metastases: melanoma, renal cell, cholangiocarcinoma, thyroid, lung. WORKUP: Chest CT (most common source), mammography, abdominal CT, tumor markers. TREATMENT: Depends on number, size, location, primary tumor type, KPS score. Single/few accessible: surgical resection or SRS (stereotactic radiosurgery). Multiple: whole brain radiation therapy (WBRT). Systemic therapy for chemosensitive tumors. Prognosis: RPA class I (KPS >=70, age <65, controlled primary, no extracranial mets) = median 7.7 months; Class III (KPS <70) = median 2 months.

callouts.text: Multiple brain lesions at gray-white junction with known primary cancer = metastases until proven otherwise

expanded_sections.heading: Prinsip Manajemen

content_blocks.text: SURGERY: Indications - accessible lesion causing mass effect, need for histological diagnosis, single metastasis, recurrent/residual after other treatment. Goals: maximal safe resection while preserving function (awake craniotomy for eloquent areas). RADIATION THERAPY: Whole brain RT (WBRT) for multiple metastases; Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS/Gamma Knife) for 1-4 small metastases or residual tumor; Fractionated RT for gliomas; Proton beam for selected cases. CHEMOTHERAPY: Temozolomide for gliomas; Methotrexate for primary CNS lymphoma; Targeted therapy (bevacizumab for GBM). SYMPTOMATIC MANAGEMENT: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone 4-10 mg q6h) for vasogenic edema - taper after definitive treatment; Antiepileptics (levetiracetam, valproate) only if seizures have occurred (not for prophylaxis); PPI for GI protection with steroids; DVT prophylaxis; Pain management.

content_blocks.text: CNS tumors account for approximately 1-2% of all cancers. Incidence increases with age, with a secondary peak in childhood. The most common primary brain tumors in adults are gliomas (50-60%), meningiomas (30-35%), and pituitary adenomas (15%). In children, the most common are pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, and ependymoma. Metastatic brain tumors are 3-10 times more common than primary brain tumors. Slight male predominance for most malignant tumors; meningiomas more common in females.

expanded_sections.heading: Klasifikasi WHO CNS5 2021
expanded_sections.subheading: WHO Classification of CNS Tumors 5th Edition

content_blocks.text: WHO CNS5 (2021) represents a paradigm shift from purely histological to INTEGRATED DIAGNOSIS combining histology and molecular markers. Key changes: Diffuse gliomas are now classified by IDH mutation status and 1p/19q codeletion; Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant vs Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted vs Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype. Glioblastoma is now restricted to IDH-wildtype tumors. New entities: Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered (previously DIPG), ATRT (atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor), embryonal tumors. Molecular markers: IDH1/2 mutation, 1p/19q codeletion, MGMT methylation (predicts temozolomide response), TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, H3F3A mutation, BRAF V600E. GRADING: CNS5 uses Arabic numerals (CNS Grade 1-4) within tumor types rather than Roman numerals across types. Grading considers histological features AND molecular markers.

content_blocks.text: SUPRATENTORIAL TUMORS: Frontal lobe (personality changes, executive dysfunction, contralateral hemiparesis, urinary incontinence, frontal release signs); Temporal lobe (memory impairment, seizures, auditory/visual hallucinations, aphasia if dominant hemisphere); Parietal lobe (contralateral sensory loss, neglect on right, Gerstmann syndrome on left, apraxia, visual field defect); Occipital lobe (contralateral homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia). INFRATENTORIAL TUMORS: Cerebellum (ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, nystagmus, hydrocephalus); Brainstem (cranial nerve palsies, long tract signs, ataxia, respiratory/cardiovascular abnormalities); Fourth ventricle (hydrocephalus, increased ICP). SELLA/SUPRASELLAR: Pituitary dysfunction (endocrine abnormalities), visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia), headache. MULTIFOCAL/METASTATIC: Multiple lesions with varying symptoms, signs of increased ICP.

content_blocks.text: GLIOBLASTOMA, IDH-WILDTYPE (WHO CNS Grade 4): Most common malignant brain tumor; peak 45-70 years; highly infiltrative; central necrosis, microvascular proliferation, pseudopalisading necrosis; treatment: maximal resection + Stupp protocol (temozolomide + RT); median survival 15 months; MGMT methylation predicts better response. MENINGIOMA (WHO Grade 1-3): Most common benign brain tumor; female predominance; progesterone receptor positive; WHO grade based on mitotic count, brain invasion, specific histological features; Simpson grading for surgical resection extent. PITUITARY ADENOMA: Prolactinoma (medical treatment with dopamine agonists - cabergoline/bromocriptine); GH-secreting (somatostatin analogs, surgery); ACTH-secreting (Cushing disease, transsphenoidal surgery); Non-functioning (surgery if mass effect). ACOUSTIC NEUROMA (VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA): CPA mass; bilateral in NF2; treatment based on size and hearing status. MEDULLOBLASTOMA: Most common malignant pediatric brain tumor; posterior fossa midline; radiosensitive; SHH, WNT, Group 3, Group 4 molecular subgroups. METASTASES: Lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colon; MRI with contrast; treatment based on number/size/primary/KPS.

callouts.text: MGMT promoter methylation in glioblastoma predicts better response to temozolomide and longer survival

expanded_sections.heading: Pendekatan Diagnostik

content_blocks.text: IMAGING HIERARCHY: CT head (first-line, exclude hemorrhage, calcification, mass effect); MRI with contrast (gold standard, characterize tumor, assess extent, surgical planning); MRI spectroscopy (elevated choline, reduced NAA, lactate/lipid peak in high-grade tumors); perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV in high-grade); PET (differentiate recurrence from radiation necrosis). INDICATIONS FOR BIOPSY: Uncertain diagnosis, inaccessible location, medical comorbidities precluding surgery, need for molecular markers. STEREOTACTIC BIOPSY: Frame-based or frameless (neuronavigation); CT or MRI guidance; sample from enhancing margin (avoid necrotic center). LUMBAR PUNCTURE: Generally contraindicated if mass effect; useful for leptomeningeal metastasis, lymphoma workup.

bullets: CT: first-line, eksklusi hemoragi
MRI dengan kontras: standar emas
Biopsi: jika diagnosis tidak pasti atau lokasi tidak terjangkau
LP: kontraindikasi jika efek massa

content_blocks.text: SURGICAL INDICATIONS: Tissue diagnosis, mass effect reduction, seizure control, hydrocephalus relief. EMERGENCIES: Herniation signs (unequal pupils, Cushing triad), acute hydrocephalus, posterior fossa tumor with brainstem compression. AWAKE CRANIOTOMY: For tumors in eloquent areas (motor, speech); allows intraoperative mapping. RADIATION: Conventional fractionated RT; SRS (Gamma Knife, CyberKnife) for small metastases and residual tumors; Proton beam for pediatric tumors. CHEMOTHERAPY: Temozolomide (oral, crosses BBB, for gliomas); PCV (procarbazine, CCNU, vincristine for oligodendroglioma); Methotrexate (for lymphoma); Bevacizumab (VEGF inhibitor, for recurrent GBM). SPECIAL POPULATIONS: PREGNANCY: Physiologic changes affect tumor behavior (meningiomas may grow); MRI without contrast preferred; delay RT if possible; steroids for edema; most chemotherapies contraindicated. IMMUNOCOMPROMISED: Consider opportunistic infections (toxoplasmosis, PML, fungal abscesses) in differential; primary CNS lymphoma common. PEDIATRIC: Different tumor spectrum; more sensitive to radiation (cognitive effects, secondary malignancies); proton therapy preferred.
